body.text: Tarkaśāstram /
body.translated_text: <s>Tarkaśāstra</s> (Treatise on Reasoning)

body.text: atha prathamaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: Now, the first chapter.

body.text: (śāstramāha) bhavān manyate 'smadvacanamanyāyyamiti cedbhavato 'pi vacanamanyāyyam / yadi bhavadvacanamanyāyyaṃ, tadāsmadvacanaṃ nyāyyam / yadi [bhavatocyate] bhavadvacanaṃ nyāyyaṃ, paramasmadvacanamanyāyyaṃ tanna yuktam / kiñca yadanyāyyaṃ tadetatsvato nyāyyaṃ, tasmād yadanyāyyaṃ tannāsti / yadi svato 'nyāyyaṃ tadetadanyāyyamasaccaiva, tasmādahamanyāyya[vādī] iti cedbhavatocyate tadayuktam /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) If you think that our statement is unreasonable, then your statement too is unreasonable. If your statement is unreasonable, then our statement is reasonable. If you say your statement is reasonable, then [you claim] our statement is unreasonable—that is not justified. Moreover, whatever is unreasonable is itself reasonable by its own nature; therefore what is unreasonable does not exist. If it is unreasonable by its own nature, then this [claim of] being unreasonable is itself non-existent; therefore, if you say "I am one who speaks unreasonably," that is unjustified.

body.text: anyacca / mama vacanamanyāyyamiti cedbhavatocyate, tato bhavānajña iti spaṣṭam / kuta iti cet / yadanyāyyaṃ tannirābhāsam / vacanaṃ nyāyābhāvādbhinnamabhinnaṃ vā ? / abhinnaṃ cedvacanamapi nāstīti mama vacanamanyāyyamiti bhavatā kathamucyate / atha bhinnaṃ, tato vacanaṃ nyāyyamiti mama vacanamanyāyyamiti kathaṃ bhavatocyate / vacanasvalakṣaṇakhaṇḍanācca / bhavatkhaṇḍanavacanamasmadvacanasya samakālīnamasamakālīnaṃ vā? samakālīnaṃ cedasmadvacanakhaṇḍane 'samarthaṃ, yathā gośṛṅge 'śvakarṇau vā parasparaṃ khaṇḍayituṃ na śaknuvataḥ / samakālīnatvāt / asamakālīnañced, bhavataḥ khaṇḍanaṃ pūrvamasmadvacanaṃ paścāt / athāsmadvacanānuccāraṇāt, kiṃ bhavatā khaṇḍyate? / tasmādbhavataḥ khaṇḍanamasidvam / athāsmadvacanaṃ (

children.translated_text: (Tarkaśāstra 4)

children.text: ) pūrvaṃ, bhavataḥ khaṇḍanaṃ tu paścād, evaṃ tarhyasmadvacanasidvatvāt kasya khaṇḍanaṃ bhaviṣyati? / samakālīnañcet, tato 'smadvacanaṃ bhavataśca khaṇḍanamityetayoretat khaṇḍanametacca khaṇḍanīyamiti viśeṣo na syāt / yathā nadīsamudravārisaṃyogakāle viśeṣāsambhavaḥ /
children.translated_text: comes first and your refutation comes afterward, then since our statement is [already] established, what will there be to refute? If [they are] simultaneous, then our statement and your refutation—between these two there would be no distinction between what is the refutation and what is to be refuted. Just as at the time of the confluence of river water and ocean water, no distinction is possible.

body.translated_text: Furthermore, if you say that my statement is unreasonable, then it is clear that you are ignorant. If you ask why, [consider:] whatever is unreasonable is without appearance. Is a statement, due to the absence of reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>), different from or identical to [reasoning]? If identical, then statement itself does not exist—so how can you say "my statement is unreasonable"? If different, then the statement is reasonable—so how can you say "my statement is unreasonable"? And because [you would be] destroying the essential characteristic of statement itself. Is your refuting statement simultaneous with our statement or non-simultaneous? If simultaneous, it is incapable of refuting our statement—just as the horns of a cow or the ears of a horse cannot destroy each other, because of their simultaneity. If non-simultaneous, [then] your refutation comes first and our statement comes afterward. But since our statement has not yet been uttered, what is being refuted by you? Therefore your refutation is unestablished. If our statement

body.text: aparañca / bhavataḥ khaṇḍanaṃ svakhaṇḍanārthamasvakhaṇḍanārthaṃ vā? svakhaṇḍanārthañcet, tataḥ svataḥ svārthahīnaṃ bhavedasmadvacananu siddham / asvakhaṇḍanārthañced, asiddham / kuta iti cet, svārthataḥ khaṇḍanāsidveḥ / siddhañcet, svārthahāniḥ parārthasidviśca /
body.translated_text: Moreover, is your refutation for the purpose of refuting itself or not for the purpose of refuting itself? If for the purpose of refuting itself, then being by its own nature devoid of its own purpose, our statement would be established. If not for the purpose of refuting itself, then it is unestablished. If you ask why: because refutation is not established from its own purpose. If it is established, there is loss of its own purpose and establishment of the other's purpose.

body.text: kiñcāsmadvacanamanyāyyamiti ced, vacanameva na bhavet / vacanañcennaivānyāyyam / anyāyyamiti cet, tadvirudvam / yathā kumārī putravatīti / yato yadi kumārī putravatīti na sampadyate / yadi putravatī, tarhi naiva kumārī / kumārīti putravatīti cobhayaṃ virudvam / tasmānmama vacanamanyāyyamiti cedbhavatocyate tadayuktam / etatpunaḥ pratyakṣavirudvam / bhavānasmākaṃ vacanaṃ śrutvānyāyyaṃ manyate cet, tattarhi śrutatvātpratyakṣasiddham / pratyakṣaṃ hi balavattaraṃ tasmādbhavadvacanahāniḥ / yathā kaścinmanyeta śrotravijñānataḥ śabdasyānupalabdhiratha śrotravijñānataḥ śabdasyopalabdhiḥ pratyakṣasidveti, tadā pratyakṣasya balavattaratvāttadvacanahāniḥ /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, if my statement is unreasonable, then there would be no statement at all. And if it is a statement, it is not at all unreasonable. If you say it is unreasonable, that is contradictory—like saying "a virgin has a son." For if she is a virgin, it does not hold that she has a son. If she has a son, then she is certainly not a virgin. "Virgin" and "having a son"—both are contradictory. Therefore, if you say my statement is unreasonable, that is unjustified. This, furthermore, contradicts direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). If you, having heard our statement, consider it unreasonable, then since it has been heard, it is established by direct perception. For direct perception is the most powerful [means of knowledge]; therefore your statement is defeated. Just as if someone were to think there is no apprehension of sound through auditory consciousness, yet there is apprehension of sound through auditory consciousness established by direct perception—then, due to the greater power of direct perception, that [contrary] statement is defeated.

body.text: anumānaviruddhaṃ caitat / mama vacanamanumānenopalabhyate cettato nyāyyamiti spaṣṭam / anyāyyaṃ hi vacanaṃ naiva vidyate / yadi vacanamasti tadā nyāyyamiti jñāyate / yathā kaścinmanyeta śabdo 'nityo hetumattvāt / yacca hetumattadanityaṃ, (

children.translated_text: (Tarkaśāstra 5)

children.text: ) yathā ghaṭaḥ / sa hetumattvādanityaḥ / yadi hetumāṃstadānityaḥ śabdo, yadi nityo naiva hetumān / ityanityatānumānasidvā / anumānabalānnityatahāniḥ / nyāyyamiti, yadvacanaṃ tannyāyyam / yannyāyyamityanumānasiddhaṃ, tadanyāyyamiti pratiṣidvam / lokavirudvaṃ caitat / yadbhavatoktaṃ mama vacanamanyāyyamiti tallokavirudvam / kasmāditi, loke hi caturvidhanyāyasatvāt / [tathā hi] hetuphalanyāyaḥ sāpekṣanyāyaḥ sādhananyāyastathatānyāyaśca /
children.translated_text: like a pot. It is impermanent because of being produced from a cause. If produced from a cause, then sound is impermanent; if permanent, it is certainly not produced from a cause. Thus impermanence is established by inference. By the force of inference, permanence is defeated. That which is reasonable—whatever statement [there is] is reasonable. That which is established by inference as reasonable—to maintain that it is unreasonable is refuted. And this contradicts the world. What you have said—"my statement is unreasonable"—that contradicts the world. Why? Because in the world there exist four types of reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>). They are: the reasoning of cause and effect (<s>hetuphalanyāya</s>), the reasoning of dependence (<s>sāpekṣanyāya</s>), the reasoning of proof (<s>sādhananyāya</s>), and the reasoning of suchness (<s>tathatānyāya</s>).

body.translated_text: And this contradicts inference (<s>anumāna</s>). If my statement is apprehended through inference, then it is clearly reasonable. For an unreasonable statement simply does not exist. If a statement exists, then it is known to be reasonable. Just as someone might think: sound is impermanent, because of being produced from a cause. And whatever is produced from a cause is impermanent,

body.text: hetuphalanyāyaḥ / yathā bījamaṅkuraśca /
body.translated_text: The reasoning of cause and effect: for example, the seed and the sprout.

body.text: sāpekṣanyāyaḥ / yathā dīrghaṃ hrasvaṃ, pitā putraḥ / sādhananyāyaḥ / yathā pañcāvayavavākyaṃ sādhanārtham / tathatānyāyastrividhaḥ / yathānātmatathatānityatātathatā nirodhatathatā ca / iha loke vacanaṃ phalaṃ, nyāyo heturiti / iha loke yadā phalaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ tadā sahetukaṃ jñātam / yadā vacanamupalabdhaṃ, tadā nyāyyaṃ jñātam / yanmama vacanamanyāyyamiti bhavatoktaṃ tallokavirudvam / anyāyyaṃ vacanamityasya nāstyavakāśaḥ /
body.translated_text: The reasoning of dependence: for example, long [depends on] short, father [depends on] son. The reasoning of proof: for example, the five-membered syllogism for the purpose of proof. The reasoning of suchness is threefold: for example, the suchness of non-self (<s>anātma</s>), the suchness of impermanence (<s>anityatā</s>), and the suchness of cessation (<s>nirodha</s>). In this world, a statement is the effect and reasoning is the cause. In this world, when an effect is seen, it is known to have a cause. When a statement is apprehended, it is known to be reasonable. What you have said—"my statement is unreasonable"—contradicts the world. For the [notion of] "an unreasonable statement" has no scope.

body.text: yad bhavatoktaṃ mama vacanamanyahisaṃvāditvāditi tadidamidānīṃ bhavatā sārdhaṃ vicārya nirdhāryate / yadi kaścidanyadvadettadā tasya doṣaḥ syat / bhidyate bhavataḥ pratijñāsmatpratijñātaḥ / atha tadbhavataḥ svoktam / tadānyaduktam / tasmādbhavāneva doṣamāpadyate / yadi bhavadartho 'smaduktādanyastadānyatvadoṣo bhavata eva na tu mama / yadi nānyat, tarhi matpakṣatulyameva, tena nāstyanyatvam / athocyate mamānyaditi tanmithyā / anyaccānyasmānnānyadityananyatvam / (

children.translated_text: (Tarkaśāstra 6)

children.text: ) yadyanyadanyasmādanyat, tato 'nyanna bhavet / yathā manuṣyo goranyo na gaurbhavati, yadyanyadanyasmādanyat, tadā tadekaṃ bhavet / yadyekaṃ tato nānyat, tatkimucyate mamānyaditi / ataścaitanyāyyamiti / ahaṃ nyāyamavalambya bhavatā vivade / tasmādanyathāhaṃ vadāmi / yadyāvayorbheda eva na syānna tadā bhavatā vivādo 'haṃ tu bhavadarthameva vadāmi /
children.translated_text: If what is different is different from another, then that other would not exist. Just as a man is different from a cow—[but then] it would not be a cow. If what is different is different from another, then that would be one [and the same]. If it is one, then it is not different—so why do you say "mine is different"? Therefore, this [claim of yours] is unreasonable. I engage in debate with you relying upon reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>). Therefore I speak otherwise. If there were no difference at all between us, then there would be no debate with you—I would simply be saying what you mean.

body.translated_text: What you have said—that my statement does not accord with others—this is now examined and determined in discussion with you. If someone else were to say something [different], then the fault would be his. Your thesis is distinguished from our thesis. But that is your own statement, and it is [itself] something different. Therefore, the fault falls upon you alone. If your meaning is different from what we have said, then the fault of otherness belongs to you alone, not to me. If it is not different, then it is equivalent to my position, and there is no otherness. If you say "mine is different," that is false. Moreover, what is different from another is not different—[since] that is non-otherness.

body.text: sarvamuktamanyaditi ced, bhavatāpi kiñciduktamiti bhavānapyanyadvadatīti doṣo bhavata eva / yadi bhavato vākyaṃ nānyat, tarhi mamāpi vacanaṃ nānyaditi yad bhavatoktamahamanyadvadāmīti tadayuktam / atha bhavadvacanaṃ mithyaiva / śeṣaṃ pūrvavat / yad (bhavato)ktaṃ mama vacanamasiddhamiti tadidānīṃ (bhavatā sārdhaṃ) vicārya nirdhāryate / yadi vacanamasiddhaṃ, tadā tadeva vacanamasiddham / yadi vacanasyāsiddhatvaṃ, tadā vacanameva na prāptam / atha vacanaṃ na prāptaṃ, kathaṃ bhavatocyate mayā yaduktaṃ tadasiddhamiti / atha vacanaṃ prāptaṃ tatsidvameva syāt / yadi maduktamasiddhamiti bhavatocyate tadayuktam / yadi sarvaṃ vacanamasiddha, tarhi bhavaduktaṃ mama khaṇdanamapyasiddham / yadi bhavaduktaṃ khaṇḍanamasiddhaṃ na syāt, tarhi mama vacanamapi naivāsiddham / yadi (bhavato)cyate maduktamasiddhaṃ tadayuktam / yadasiddhaṃ tatsvata eva siddham / tasmānnāstyasiddham / yadyasiddha na svataḥ siddhaṃ, tadāsiddhaṃ na syāt / yadi siddhaṃ, nāstyasiddhaṃ, tato yad (bhavato)ktaṃ maduktamasiddhamiti tanniravakāśam / yadi bhavatocyate mama khaṇḍanamananubhāṣaṇameva tadā na mama matasyopalabdhi / (

children.translated_text: (Tarkaśāstra 7)

children.text: ) atha nopalabhyate mama mataṃ, tato mama khaṇḍanaṃ kartuṃ na śakyate / tadidānīṃ (bhavatā sārdhaṃ)vicārya nirdhāryate / yadi bhavān matkhaṇḍanaṃ nānubhāṣate, tadā bhavān khaṇḍanaṃ vaktuṃ na śaknoti / kiṃ punarmanyate bhavān khaṇḍanamananubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ śakyaṃ, athavā khaṇḍanamanubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ śakyam / yadi tāvad (bhavān) ananubhāṣya (khaṇḍanaṃ vaktuṃ śaknoti), ahamapyananubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ vaktuṃ śaknuyām / athavā khaṇḍanamanubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ vaktuṃ śakyaṃ, tadā sadaiva khaṇḍanānubhāṣaṇam syāt / kutaḥ? khaṇḍanātpunaḥ khaṇḍanasyotpannatvāt / tadā khaṇḍanānavasthā / na ca sa kālo vidyate yatra na khaṇḍanānubhāṣaṇam / [ataḥ] yatra khaṇḍanaṃ vaktuṃ śakyate sa kālo nāsti /
children.translated_text: ) Now, if my thesis is not apprehended, then it is impossible for you to refute me. Now, let this be examined and determined [in discussion] with you. If you do not repeat (<s>anubhāṣaṇa</s>) my refutation, then you are unable to state a refutation. What indeed do you think—is refutation possible without repeating [the opponent's position], or is refutation possible [only] by repeating [it]? If you can state a refutation without repeating [it], then I too could state a refutation without repeating [it]. Or if refutation is possible [only] by repeating the refutation, then there would always be a repetition of refutation. Why? Because from a refutation, yet another refutation arises. Then there would be an infinite regress of refutations. And there is no time at which repetition of refutation does not [occur]. [Therefore] there is no time at which it is possible to state a refutation.

body.translated_text: If you say everything said is different, then since you too have said something, you too are saying something different—so the fault is yours alone. If your statement is not different, then my statement too is not different, and so what you have said—"I am saying something different"—is unjustified. Otherwise, your statement itself is simply false. The rest is as before. What you have said—"my statement is unestablished"—this is now examined and determined in discussion with you. If a statement is unestablished, then that very statement [of yours] is unestablished. If a statement has the quality of being unestablished, then no statement has been obtained at all. If no statement has been obtained, how can you say "what I have said is unestablished"? If a statement has been obtained, then it would be established. If you say my statement is unestablished, that is unjustified. If all statements are unestablished, then your stated refutation of me is also unestablished. If your stated refutation would not be unestablished, then my statement too is certainly not unestablished. If you say my statement is unestablished, that is unjustified. Whatever is unestablished is established by its own nature. Therefore, there is nothing unestablished. If the unestablished is not established by its own nature, then it would not be unestablished. If it is established, there is nothing unestablished; therefore what you have said—"my statement is unestablished"—has no scope. If you say your refutation [consists in] simply not responding, then there is no apprehension of my position.

body.text: aparañca khaṇḍanamiti khaṇḍanānnāma / yadi tatkhaṇḍanānubhāṣaṇānnāma khaṇḍanamiti vaktuṃ śakyate, ananubhāṣya tu khaṇḍanamiti vaktuṃ ja śakyate / tataḥ pūrvakhaṇḍanasya nāma paścādanubhāṣaṇaṃ prāptam / paravartikhaṇḍanaṃ nāma na tāvadanubhāṣaṇaṃ prāpnoti / tṛtīyantu dvitīyasya khaṇḍanasya nāmānubhāṣaṇaṃ prāptam / caturthaṃ tṛtīyasya khaṇḍanasya nāmānubhāṣaṇaṃ prāptam / iti sadānubhāṣaṇādanavasthā / ananubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ nāma vaktuṃ śakyamiti ced, ananubhāṣyāpi tataḥ prathamaṃ khaṇḍanaṃ nāma vaktuṃ śakyam / prathamaṃ khaṇḍanam nāmānanubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ nāma vaktuṃ śakyamiti cet, dvitīyamapi khaṇḍanaṃ nāmānanubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ nāma vaktuṃ śakyate / dvitīyaṃ khaṇḍanaṃ nāmānanubhāṣya khaṇḍanamiti vaktuṃ śakyata iti cet, prathamaṃ khaṇḍanaṃ (

children.translated_text: Tś 8

children.text: ) nāmāpyananubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ nāma vaktuṃ śakyeta / kintu prathamaṃ khaṇḍanaṃ nāmāvaśyamanubhāṣyam / tasmātkhaṇḍanaṃ nāma vaktuṃ śakyate / atha dvitīyaṃ khaṇḍanaṃ nāmāpyavaśyamanubhāṣyaṃ, tadā khaṇḍanaṃ nāma vaktuaṃ śakyate natvananubhāṣya vaktavyam / yadi punaḥ khaṇḍanamananubhāṣya vadet, khaṇḍanasya nigrahasthānāpattiḥ / yadi bhavān svakhaṇḍanaṃ nānubhāṣate, tato bhavaduktakhaṇḍanasya nigrahasthānāpattiḥ / yadi bhavān khaṇḍanamananubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ vadet, khaṇḍanaṃ vadaṃśca nigrahasthāne na patet, tadāhamapi khaṇḍanamananubhāṣya khaṇḍanaṃ vadanna nigrāhyaḥ / kiñca yadā bhavadvacanaṃ mama[mataṃ] khaṇḍayati, tadāhamanubhāṣe / yadā tvahaṃ bhavanmataṃ khaṇḍayāmi tadā bhavānapyanubhāṣate / atha parasparānubhāṣaṇaṃ, na tadā khaṇḍanapratiṣṭhāpanam / yadi parasparānubhāṣaṇaṃ, tadā samyagarthahāniḥ / yathā potāvanyonyasambadvau samudravelāsamaye parasparasaṃgharṣeṇa dolāyamānau /
children.translated_text: ) could also be stated as 'refutation' without repeating [it]. However, the name of the first refutation must necessarily be repeated. Therefore, one is able to state a refutation. Now, if the name of the second refutation also must necessarily be repeated, then one can state a refutation, but not without repeating [it]. If, however, one were to state a refutation without repeating [it], there would be a defeat-situation (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>) for the refutation. If you do not repeat your own refutation, then there is a defeat-situation for the refutation you have stated. If you were to state a refutation without repeating the refutation, and in stating the refutation not fall into a defeat-situation, then I too, stating a refutation without repeating [it], would not be subject to censure. Moreover, when your statement refutes my thesis, then I repeat [it]. And when I refute your thesis, then you also repeat [it]. Now, if there is mutual repetition, then there is no establishment of the refutation. If there is mutual repetition, then both sides lose their correct meaning—like two boats bound together at the time of an ocean flood, tossing about from mutual collision.

body.translated_text: Furthermore, 'refutation' is so named after a refutation. If one can say 'refutation' only after repeating the refutation, but cannot say 'refutation' without repeating [it], then the name of the first refutation requires subsequent repetition. The second refutation, however, does not yet require repetition. But the third requires the repetition of the name of the second refutation. The fourth requires the repetition of the name of the third refutation. Thus, from constant repetition, there is an infinite regress. If it is said that one can state the name 'refutation' without repeating [it], then one can also state the name 'refutation' for the first [refutation] without repeating [it]. If it is said that one can state the name of a refutation without repeating the name of the first refutation, then one can also state the name of the second refutation without repeating the name of the refutation. If it is said that one can state 'refutation' without repeating the name of the second refutation, then the first refutation (

body.text: aparañca / sarve śabdā yadā mukhānnirgatāstadā naṣṭā eveti kathaṃ madvacanānubhāṣaṇam? / atha śabdo vināśadharmā / apunarāgamanātpunarbhāṣaṇamaśakyam / atha śabdaḥ sthitiśīlastadānubhāṣaṇamaśakyaṃ, nityatvāt / naṣṭa iti cen, na kiñcidanubhāṣitavyaṃ tadabhāvāt / śabdo naṣṭa iti cet, tvadanubhāṣaṇāyaitanme vacanamiti yadbhavān bravīti sa kutarka eva /
body.translated_text: Furthermore: all words, when they have issued from the mouth, are already destroyed—so how can there be repetition of my statement? Now, a word is of a perishable nature. Since it does not return, re-statement is impossible. Now, if a word is of a stable nature, then repetition is impossible, because [it would be] permanent. If [you say] it is destroyed, then nothing is to be repeated, because of its non-existence. If [you say] the word is destroyed, then your saying 'this is my statement for your repetition' is mere sophistry (<s>kutarka</s>).

body.text: yad (bhavato)ktaṃ madvacanaṃ pūrva, [bhavata] khaṇḍanaṃ tu paścāditi tadidānīṃ (bhavatā sārdhaṃ) vicārya nirdhāryate / yadi madvacanaṃ pūrvaṃ, khaṇḍanantu paścāditi tanyāyyam / kuta iti (

children.translated_text: Tś 9

children.text: ) cen, madvacanaṃ pūrvaṃ bhavadvacanaṃ tu paścāditi / yadyasmadvacanaṃ paravartivacanaṃ khaṇḍayati, tato 'smadartho viśiṣyate bhavadvacanasya tu hāniḥ / kiñca yadyucyate bhavatā sarvāṇi vacanāni pūrvavartīni khaṇḍanantu paravartīti, tadā bhavānapi pūrvameva vacanaṃ vadatīti paścātkhaṇḍanaṃ bhavet / yadi bhavadvacanasya pūrvavartitve 'pi paścātkhaṇḍanaṃ nāsti, tarhi madvacanasya pūrvavartitve 'pi, paścātkhaṇḍanaṃ na syāt / yacca khaṇḍanaṃ pūrvasya paravartīti svabhāvataḥ pūrvasya khaṇḍanaṃ na paścādasti / yadi svabhāvata eva pūrvasya khaṇḍanaṃ paścāt syāt, tadā pūrvaṃ paścādityubhe na syātām / tasmādyadbhavatoktaṃ pūrvasya khaṇḍanaṃ parabhāvīti tadayuktam / yadi svabhāvataḥ pūrvasya khaṇḍanaṃ na paścāt / hetvabhāvāt / tadā pūrvasyāpi khaṇḍanaṃ parabhāvi na bhavet / yadbhavatoktaṃ madvacanaṃ pūrvaṃ, khaṇḍanaṃ tu parabhāvi tanmithyā /
children.translated_text: ) Because my statement comes first and your statement comes later. If the subsequent statement refutes our [prior] statement, then our meaning prevails, but your statement suffers loss. Moreover, if you say that all statements come first and refutation comes later, then you too first state a statement, and the refutation would come afterward. If even when your statement comes first there is no subsequent refutation, then even when my statement comes first, there should be no subsequent refutation. And as for the refutation being subsequent to the prior [statement]—by its very nature, the refutation of the prior [statement] does not exist afterward. If by its very nature the refutation of the prior were to exist afterward, then 'prior' and 'posterior' would both cease to be. Therefore, what you have said—that the refutation of the prior comes subsequently—is improper. If by nature the refutation of the prior does not come afterward—because of the absence of a reason—then even the refutation of the prior would not come subsequently. What you have said, 'My statement comes first, but the refutation comes subsequently,' is false.

body.translated_text: As for what you have said, 'My statement comes first, but your refutation comes later'—let this now be examined and determined [in discussion] with you. If my statement comes first and the refutation comes later, that is not proper. Why? (

body.text: yadabhihitaṃ bhavatā, mayā hetvantaramuktamiti tadidānīṃ (bhavatā sārdhaṃ) vicārya nirdhāryate / yadi pūrvahetuṃ parityajya hetvantarapratiṣṭhāpanānnigrahasthānamāpadyate, tadā bhavān nigrahasthānamāpannaḥ / kathamiti ced, bhavatā pūrvahetuṃ parityajya hetvantarapratiṣṭhāpanāt / yadi hetvantarapratiṣṭhāpanādbhavato na nigrahasthānatvāpattistadā mamāpi tathā / kiñca maduktahetuto bhavaduktahetorbhedaḥ / yadyanyaṃ hetuṃ vadāmi tanmama nyāyyam / yadyanyaṃ hetuṃ na vadeyaṃ, tato bhavaddhetuṃ vadeyam / tato na pratipakṣatayā virodho 'pi tvāvayostulyavacanataiva / yadi sadṛśa eva heturāvābhyāṃ pratiṣṭhāpitaḥ, tadā bhavānasmaddhetuṃ khaṇḍayatīti svahetumeva khaṇḍayati /
body.translated_text: As for what you have stated, 'I have stated a different reason'—let this now be examined and determined [in discussion] with you. If, by abandoning the prior reason and establishing a different reason, one incurs a defeat-situation (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>), then you have incurred a defeat-situation. How so? Because you have abandoned the prior reason and established a different reason. If establishing a different reason does not entail a defeat-situation for you, then the same applies to me. Moreover, your stated reason differs from my stated reason. If I state a different reason, that is proper for me. If I were not to state a different reason, then I would be stating your reason. In that case, there would be no opposition between us as adversaries—rather, we would be making the same statement. If the very same reason has been established by both of us, then when you refute our reason, you refute your own reason.

body.text: api ca yadi sarvāṇi vacanāni hetvantarāṇi syustadābhavaduktāni vacanānyapi hetvantarāṇi bhaveyuḥ / tataśca bhavato nigrahasthānāpattiḥ / atha vacanānyuccārayannapi na bhavān nigrāhyastarhi yadbhavatoktaṃ hetuṃ pratiṣṭhāpayannahaṃ nigrāhya iti tadayuktam /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, if all statements were to be different reasons, then the statements made by you would also be different reasons. And then there would be a defeat-situation for you. But if, even while uttering statements, you are not subject to censure, then what you have said—that I am subject to censure while establishing a reason—is improper.

body.text: yadbhavatoktamarthāntaraṃ vadāmīti tadidānīṃ (bhavatā sārdhaṃ) vicāryaṃ nirdhāryate / anyā me pratijñā, anyā ca bhavata iti yattannyāyyameva / athāhaṃ bhavataḥ pratipakṣatayā virodhītyarthāntaraṃ bravīmi / yadi matamasmadartho bhavadarthādananyastadāsmadartho bhavadarthapratipakṣatayā na virudvo / yadi bhavānasmadarthaṃ khaṇḍayati, tarhi bhavataḥ svārthasyaiva khaṇḍanaṃ bhavet / yadarthāntaraṃ na tatsvayamarthāntarama / tasmānnāstyarthāntaram / yadi tvarthāntaraṃ svayamevārthāntaraṃ, na tadārthāntaram / tasmādyadbhavatoktamahamarthāntaraṃ vadāmīti na yuktam / aparañca yaduktaṃ sarvaṃ tadarthāntarañcettadā bhavaduktamapyarthāntaraṃ bhavet / yadi bhavaduktamarthāntaraṃ na bhavettadā yadbhavatā pratijñātaṃ sarvamarthāntaramiti tadayuktam /
body.translated_text: As for what you have said, 'You are stating an irrelevant topic (<s>arthāntara</s>)'—let this now be examined and determined [in discussion] with you. That my thesis is different from yours—that is indeed proper. Now, I speak as one opposed to you as an adversary, and [so I raise] a different topic. If it is accepted that our meaning is not different from your meaning, then our meaning is not opposed to your meaning as an adversary. If you refute our meaning, then you would be refuting your own meaning. What is a different topic is not itself inherently a different topic. Therefore, there is no different topic. But if a different topic were itself inherently a different topic, it would not [really] be a different topic. Therefore, what you have said, 'I state a different topic,' is not proper. Furthermore, if everything stated is a different topic, then what you have stated would also be a different topic. If what you have stated is not a different topic, then your claim that 'everything is a different topic' is improper.

body.text: yad (bhavato)ktamahaṃ pūrvacanādananyadvacanaṃ vadāmīti tadidānīṃ (bhavatā sārdhaṃ) vicārya nirdhāryate / asmatpratijñā bhavatpratijñāyāḥ pratipakṣabhāvena viruddhā / yadasmatpratijñā bhavatpratijñāyāḥ pratipakṣabhāvena virudvā, tannyāyyam / kuta iti cet / sarvatrāhaṃ bhavadarthakhaṇḍanārthaṃ vadāmi, tasmādasmadvacanamananyat / yadi mayārthāntaramuktaṃ, tarhi bhavatpratijñāsmadarthādanyā / yadyahamarthāntaraṃ vadāmi tadā (

children.translated_text: Tś 11

children.text: ) bhavadarthaṃ vadāmi / evantāvannāhaṃ bhavadviruddo / tataśca yadi bhavān māṃ khaṇḍayati, tarhi svārthasyaiva khaṇḍanam /
children.translated_text: ) I am stating your meaning. In that case, I am indeed not opposed to you. And therefore, if you refute me, you would be refuting your own meaning.

body.translated_text: As for what you have said, 'I state a statement not different from the prior statement'—let this now be examined and determined [in discussion] with you. Our thesis is opposed to your thesis by way of being a counter-thesis. That our thesis is opposed to your thesis by way of being a counter-thesis is proper. Why? Because everywhere I speak for the purpose of refuting your meaning; therefore our statement is not different [from the topic]. If I were to state a different topic, then your thesis would be different from our meaning. If I state a different topic, then (

body.text: anyacca / yathā mayā pūrvamuktamanityaḥ śabda iti / etāni vacanāni vināśasvabhāvāni kṣayasvabhāvāni ca / idānīmanyadvacanamuccaryate / tataśca yadbhavatoktaṃ bhavān pūrvavacanaṃ vadatīti tanmithyā /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, as I previously said 'sound is impermanent' — these words [themselves] are of a nature that perishes and decays. Now a different utterance is produced. Therefore, your statement that 'you are saying your previous statement' is false.

body.text: aparañca / yadbhavatoktaṃ maduktamananyaditi / tatra yadyahamanyadvadāmi tadā tadanyayat / yadyahamananyadvadāmi tadananyat / yadyahaṃ tadvadaṃstanna sādhayituṃ śaknomi, tadā yadbhavatoktamananyaditi tadyuktam / yacca (bhavato)ktaṃ mayā sarvamuktaṃ nānujñāyata iti tadidānīṃ (bhavatā sārdhaṃ) vicārya nirdhāryate / sarvaṃ nānujñāyata iti yaduktaṃ bhavatā etadvacanaṃ sarvasminnantarbhavati na vā? / yadi tāvatsarvasminnantarbhavati tadā bhavān svayaṃ svoktaṃ nānujānāti / yadi svayaṃ nānujānātyasmadarthaḥ svata eva siddho bhavedbhavavacanasya tu hāniḥ syāt / atha sarvasminnāntarbhavati tadā tasya sarvatvameva na syāt / yadi sarvatvameva na bhavet, tadā bhavatā yadananujñātaṃ tatsarvam / yadi sarvamananujñātaṃ tadāsmadartho bhavatā naivānanujñātaḥ / asmadarthaḥ siddho bhavatastu sarvasya pratiṣedhaḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, as to your statement 'what I said is not different [from what I say now]' — therein, if I say something different, then that [is indeed] different; if I say something not different, then [it is indeed] not different. If I, having said that, am unable to establish it, then your statement 'it is not different' is proper. And as to your statement 'nothing said by me is approved' — now this will be examined and determined in discussion with you. The statement you made 'nothing is approved' — does this statement itself fall within the scope of 'nothing' or not? If it falls within the scope of 'nothing,' then you yourself do not approve your own statement. If you yourself do not approve it, then our position would be established by itself, while your statement would suffer loss. But if it does not fall within the scope of 'nothing,' then the very 'all'-ness [of 'nothing'] would not obtain. If 'all'-ness does not obtain, then what you have not approved is everything [else]. If everything [else] is not approved, then our position has indeed not been unapproved by you. Our position is established, while your rejection of everything [fails].

body.text: iti prathamaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: Thus ends the first section.

body.text: atha dvitīyaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: Now the second section.

body.text: (śāstramāha) khaṇḍanasya trividhadoṣāpattiḥ / viparīnakhaṇḍanamasatkhaṇḍanaṃ viruddhakhaṇḍanañceti / yadi khaṇḍanametattrividhadoṣopetaṃ tadā nigrahasthānam /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) Refutation (<s>khaṇḍana</s>) is subject to three types of fault: reversed refutation (<s>viparīta-khaṇḍana</s>), baseless refutation (<s>asat-khaṇḍana</s>), and contradictory refutation (<s>viruddha-khaṇḍana</s>). If a refutation is afflicted by these three types of fault, then it constitutes a point of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>).

body.text: [tatra] viparītakhaṇḍanam / yadi pratiṣṭhāpitaṃ khaṇḍanaṃ samyagarthena na saṃyuktaṃ syāttadā tadviparītakhaṇḍanamityucyate / viparītakhaṇḍanaṃ daśavidham / (1)sādharmyakhaṇḍanam (2) vaidharmyakhaṇḍanam (3) vikalpakhaṇḍanam (4) aviśeṣakhaṇḍanam (5) prāptyaprāptikhaṇḍanam (6) ahetukhaṇḍanam(7) upalabdhikhaṇḍanam (8) saṃśayakhaṇḍanam (9) anuktikhaṇḍanam (10) kāryabhedakhaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: Therein, reversed refutation (<s>viparīta-khaṇḍana</s>): If an established refutation is not connected with a valid meaning, then it is called reversed refutation. Reversed refutation is of ten kinds: (1) refutation by similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>), (2) refutation by dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>), (3) refutation by differentiation (<s>vikalpa</s>), (4) refutation by non-distinction (<s>aviśeṣa</s>), (5) refutation by attainment and non-attainment (<s>prāptyaprāpti</s>), (6) refutation by absence of reason (<s>ahetu</s>), (7) refutation by perception (<s>upalabdhi</s>), (8) refutation by doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>), (9) refutation by non-statement (<s>anukti</s>), (10) refutation by difference of effect (<s>kāryabheda</s>).

body.text: 1. [tatra] sādharmyakhaṇḍanam / vastusādharmyapratyavasthānaṃ sādharmyakhaṇḍanamityucyate /
body.translated_text: 1. Therein, refutation by similarity (<s>sādharmya-khaṇḍana</s>): A counter-argument based on similarity of things is called refutation by similarity.

body.text: (śāstramāha) śabdo 'nityaḥ pratyanotpannatvādyathā ghaṭaḥ prayatnotpannaḥ / utpannaśca vinaṣṭaḥ / śabdo 'pi tatheti śabdo 'nitya iti sthāpite prativādī prāha / yadi ghaṭasādharmyācchabdo 'nityastadākāśasādharmyācchabdo nityaḥ syāt / tataścākāśavacchabdo nitya iti / [atra] sādharmyamamūrtatvam /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) Sound is impermanent because it is produced by effort, like a pot — [a pot] is produced by effort and, having arisen, it perishes; sound is likewise — thus when the impermanence of sound is established, the opponent (<s>prativādin</s>) says: 'If sound is impermanent due to similarity with a pot, then sound would be permanent due to similarity with space. Therefore, sound is permanent like space.' The similarity [claimed] here is incorporeality (<s>amūrtatva</s>).

body.text: (śāstraṃ punarāha) śabdo 'nityaḥ prayatnotpannatvāt / yannityaṃ na tatprayatnenotpannaṃ yathākāśaṃ nityaṃ na prayatnenotpannam / śabdastu na tathā / tasmācchabdo 'nitya iti sthāpite prativādī prāha / yadi (śabdasya) nityākāśavaidharmyacchabdo 'nitya iti, tadā kiṃ prāptam? / yadyākāśasādharmyaṃ (

children.translated_text: [<s>Tarkaśāstra</s> 13]

children.text: ) tato nitya eva śabda iti / sādharmyaṃ cāmūrtatvaṃ tasmānnityaḥ /
children.translated_text: then sound is indeed permanent. And the similarity is incorporeality; therefore [sound is] permanent.'

body.translated_text: (The treatise further says:) Sound is impermanent because it is produced by effort. What is permanent is not produced by effort, like space — space is permanent and not produced by effort. But sound is not like that. Therefore sound is impermanent. When this is established, the opponent says: 'If sound is impermanent due to dissimilarity from permanent space, then what follows? If [there is] similarity with space,

body.text: (śāstramāha) ete khaṇḍane viparīte 'siddhe ca (khaṇḍane) / kuta iti cet / aikāntikaikarasadharmasthāpanaṃ hi heturiti manyate / sarvadharmāṇāṃ prayatnotpannatvenānityatāvarṇanāt / so 'nityatāvarṇakaheturaikāntikaikarasastasmādanityatānapasaraṇīyaiva / tatsāmānajātīyaṃ cikhyāpayiṣatayā ghaṭādyudāharaṇamuktam /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) These refutations are reversed and unestablished. Why? Because it is considered that a reason (<s>hetu</s>) is one that establishes a property that is exclusively and uniformly [present] (<s>aikāntika-ekarasa</s>). Since impermanence is described through the fact that all [produced things] are produced by effort, that reason which describes impermanence is exclusively and uniformly [applicable]; therefore impermanence cannot be evaded. The example of a pot etc. is stated in order to illustrate what is of the same class (<s>sāmānajātīya</s>) as that.

body.text: prativādī tvanaikāntikaikarasārthapratyavasthānena khaṇḍanaṃ bhāṣate yathā yadi bhavān sādharmyeṇa śabdasyānityatāṃ sthāpayati tadāhamapi vaidharmyeṇa śabdasya nityatāṃ pratiṣṭhāpayāmi / yadi ca bhavadarthaḥ siddho mamāpyarthaḥ siddho bhavediti /
body.translated_text: But the opponent speaks a refutation by counter-arguing with a meaning that is not exclusively and uniformly [applicable] (<s>anaikāntika-ekarasa</s>), as follows: 'If you establish the impermanence of sound by similarity, then I too will establish the permanence of sound by dissimilarity. And if your position is established, my position too should be established.'

body.text: (śāstramāha) bhavataḥ khaṇḍanamayuktam / kuta iti cet / bhavatprayuktasya hetoranaikāntikanityatvānityatvāvyāptivarṇanāt / asmābhistrilakṣaṇo hetuḥ sthāpitaḥ / tadyathā pakṣadharmmaḥ sapakṣasatvaṃ vipakṣavyāvṛttiśca / tasmādvetusiddhiranapasaraṇīyā / bhavaddhetustu na tathā tasmādbhavatkhaṇḍanaṃ viparītam / yadi bhavatā pratiṣṭhāpito heturasmaddhetutulyobhavettadā samyakkhaṇḍanaṃ sidhyeta / yadyanityatāpratijñā nityatāṃ khaṇḍayati tadā [nityatā-] khaṇḍanasiddhiḥ / kuta iti cet / nityatāsthāpakahetunānityatāsthāpakahetuḥ khaṇḍyate cet, tadānityatāviparyāsadoṣo vyaktīkartuṃ na śakyata iti prasiddham / nityatāhetoranaikāntikaikarasatvādanityatāhetoraikāntikaikarasatvācca /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) Your refutation is improper. Why? Because the reason employed by you describes non-pervasion (<s>avyāpti</s>) of both permanence and impermanence, being non-exclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). We have established a reason with three characteristics (<s>trilakṣaṇa hetu</s>): namely, being a property of the subject (<s>pakṣadharma</s>), presence in the similar instances (<s>sapakṣasattva</s>), and exclusion from the dissimilar instances (<s>vipakṣavyāvṛtti</s>). Therefore the establishment of the reason cannot be evaded. But your reason is not like that; therefore your refutation is reversed. If the reason established by you were equal to our reason, then a correct refutation would be achieved. If the thesis of impermanence refutes permanence, then the refutation of permanence is established. Why? Because if the reason establishing permanence could refute the reason establishing impermanence, then it is well known that the fault of the reversal of impermanence cannot be demonstrated — since the reason for permanence is not exclusively and uniformly [applicable], while the reason for impermanence is exclusively and uniformly [applicable].

body.text: 2. vaidharmyakhaṇḍanam / vastuvaidharmyapratyavasthānaṃ vaidharmyakhaṇḍanamityucyate /
body.translated_text: 2. Refutation by dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya-khaṇḍana</s>): A counter-argument based on dissimilarity of things is called refutation by dissimilarity.

body.text: (śāstramāha) anityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt? kṛtakatvāt / yat kṛtakaṃ tadanityam / yathākāśaṃ nityamakṛtakatvāt / śabdasya tathātvābhāvācchabdo 'nityaḥ /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) Sound is impermanent. Why? Because it is produced (<s>kṛtaka</s>). What is produced is impermanent. As space is permanent because it is not produced (<s>akṛtaka</s>). Since sound is not like that, sound is impermanent.

body.text: prativādī prāha / yadi śabdo nityākāśavidharmyādanitya iti, tadā kiṃ prāptam / yadi ghaṭavaidharmyaṃ śabdasya, tadā sa nitya iti / tadvaidharmyamamūrtatvam / ghaṭo mūrtastasmādghaṭo 'nityaḥ śabdastu nityaḥ /
body.translated_text: The opponent says: 'If sound is impermanent due to dissimilarity from permanent space, then what follows? If [there is] dissimilarity between sound and a pot, then it [sound] is permanent. That dissimilarity is incorporeality. A pot is corporeal; therefore a pot is impermanent, but sound is permanent.'

body.text: (śāstramāha) śabdo 'nityaḥ kṛtakatvāt / yathā ghaṭo 'nityaḥ kṛtakatvāt, tathā śabdo 'pi /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) Sound is impermanent because it is produced (<s>kṛtaka</s>), just as a pot is impermanent because it is produced — so too is sound.

body.text: prativādī prāha / yadi ghaṭasādharmyācchabdasyānityatā bhavatā sthāpitā, tadā kiṃ prāptam? / śabdo nitya eva ghaṭavaidharmyādvaidharmyamamūrtatvam / ghaṭastu mūrtaḥ /
body.translated_text: The opponent says: 'If the impermanence of sound is established by you through similarity with a pot, then what follows? Sound is indeed permanent due to dissimilarity from a pot; the dissimilarity is incorporeality, and a pot is corporeal.'

body.text: (śāstramāha) viparīta ete khaṇḍane / kuta iti cet / asmatsthāpitānityatāhetoraikāntikaikarasatvāt / bhavatpratiṣṭhāpitanityatāhetostvanaikāntikaikarasatvānnityatvānityatvavyāptivarṇanāt / tasmādaniścitaheturaikāntikahetuṃ khaṇḍayituṃ na śaknoti / yo 'smābhiḥ sthāpito hetuḥ kṛtakatvācchabdo 'nitya iti tasya (hetoḥ) pakṣadharmmaḥ sapakṣasattvaṃ vipakṣavyāvṛttiśca / trayalakṣaṇasampannatvāt so 'napasaraṇīyaḥ / yaḥ punarbhavatpratiṣṭhāpito hetuḥ śabdo nityo 'mūrtatvāditi tasya pakṣadharmaḥ sapakṣe vipakṣe ca vartata ityasiddho hetuḥ /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) These refutations are reversed. Why? Because the reason established by us for impermanence is exclusively and uniformly [applicable] (<s>aikāntika-ekarasa</s>), while the reason established by you for permanence is not exclusively and uniformly [applicable], since it describes pervasion of both permanence and impermanence. Therefore an indeterminate reason (<s>aniścita-hetu</s>) cannot refute a determinate reason (<s>aikāntika-hetu</s>). The reason established by us — 'sound is impermanent because it is produced' — has the three characteristics: being a property of the subject (<s>pakṣadharma</s>), presence in the similar instances (<s>sapakṣasattva</s>), and exclusion from the dissimilar instances (<s>vipakṣavyāvṛtti</s>). Being endowed with the three characteristics, it cannot be evaded. But the reason established by you — 'sound is permanent because it is incorporeal' — is present in both the similar and dissimilar instances, and is therefore an unestablished reason (<s>asiddha-hetu</s>).

body.text: 3. vikalpakhaṇḍanam / sādharmye vaidharmyapratyavasthānaṃ vikalpakhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 3. Refutation by differentiation (<s>vikalpa-khaṇḍana</s>): A counter-argument [introducing] dissimilarity against [an argument based on] similarity is called refutation by differentiation.

body.text: (śāstramāha) śabdo 'nityaḥ pratyatnenotpannatvādghaṭavaditi śabdasyānityatā /
body.translated_text: (The treatise says:) Sound is impermanent because it is produced by effort, like a pot — thus the impermanence of sound [is established].

body.text: prativādī prāha / bhavāñchabdasya prayatnenotpannatvādghaṭavatsādharmyaṃ sthāpayati / asti punastadvaidharmyam / pakkatvamapakvatvaṃ, cākṣuṣatvamacākṣuṣatvamityādi evaṃ ghaṭaśabdayoḥ pratyekaṃ viśeṣaḥ / śabdaḥ prayatnenotpannatvānnityaḥ ghaṭastu prayatnenotpanno 'pyanityaḥ / tasmācchabdo nityaḥ /
body.translated_text: The opponent says: 'You establish similarity of sound with a pot through being produced by effort. But there is also dissimilarity between them: cookedness and uncookedness, visibility and invisibility, etc. — thus each of the pot and sound has distinctive features. Sound, though produced by effort, is permanent; but a pot, though produced by effort, is impermanent. Therefore sound is permanent.'

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanam / kuta iti cet / asmatsthāpitaheturanityatāvyāvṛtto nityatāvyāvṛttaḥ / etaddhetusthāpanamanityatānumānārtham / yathāgnyanumānārthaṃ dhūmaḥ prayujyate / dhūmo hyagnyavyāvṛttaḥ / tasmādasmatsthāpitahetuḥ sidvo 'napasaraṇīyaśca /
body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. Why? The reason established by us is confined to impermanence and excluded from permanence. This establishment of the reason is for the purpose of inferring impermanence, just as smoke is employed for the purpose of inferring fire. For smoke is confined to [the presence of] fire. Therefore the reason established by us is valid and cannot be evaded.

body.text: bhavatā śabdasyāpakva iti viśeṣaṇaṃ prayujyate / tataśca nitya iti / tadecchādveṣaduḥkhasukhavāyvādīnyapakvāni na punaretāni nityāni / tasmādapakvatvaṃ nityatāhetutvena na pratiṣṭhāpayitavyam / na cācākṣuṣatvamapi nityatāhetutvena pratiṣṭhāpayitavyam / kuta iti cet / icchadveṣaduḥkhasukhavāyvādīnyacākṣuṣāṇi na punarnityāni / bhavaddhetuḥ sapakṣe vipakṣe ca vartate tasmādasādhakaḥ / bhavaddheturmama (heto) stulyo matpratijñāyāśca khaṇḍanāsamartha iti cet / asmatsthāpanaṃ trividhahetusamāśritaṃ tasmādatulyam / yadatulyaṃ tulyamiti bhavatoktaṃ tasmādbhavataḥ khaṇḍanaṃ viparītam /
body.translated_text: You apply the qualifier "uncooked" to sound, and from that [infer] it is permanent. But then desire, aversion, suffering, pleasure, wind, and so on are also uncooked, yet these are not permanent. Therefore, the property of being uncooked should not be established as a reason for permanence. Nor should the property of being invisible be established as a reason for permanence. If you ask why: desire, aversion, suffering, pleasure, wind, and so on are invisible, yet they are not permanent. Your reason operates in both the <s>sapakṣa</s> (similar instance) and the <s>vipakṣa</s> (dissimilar instance), and therefore it is inconclusive. If you say that your reason is equal to my reason and is incapable of refuting my thesis—our establishment relies on a threefold reason, and therefore it is not equal. What is unequal you have called equal—therefore your refutation is reversed.

body.text: 4. aviśeṣakhaṇḍanam / ekasādharmyakhyāpanātsarvasyāviśeṣeṇa pratyavasthānamaviśeṣakhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 4. <s>Aviśeṣakhaṇḍana</s> (refutation by non-distinction). The objection that, from the declaration of one common property, everything without distinction should follow—this is called refutation by non-distinction.

body.text: śabdo 'nityaḥ kāraṇabhedena śabdasya bhedāddīpavat / (

children.text: ) yadi vartikā mahatī jyotirmahat / yadi vartikā kṣudrā jyotirapi kṣudram, iti sthāpite / prativādī prāha yadi sādharmyādyathā ghaṭādyanityaṃ śabdo 'pi tathā syāttadā sarvasya sarveṇāviśeṣaprasaṅgaḥ / kuta iti cet / sarvasya sarveṇa sādharmyāt / sādharmyaṃ kiṃ punaścet / sattaikatvaṃ prameyatvamityetat sādharmyamucyate / sadharmāṇyapi sarvāṇi vastūni viśeṣṭavastubhyo bhinnānīti cecchabdo 'pi tathā / ghaṭādisadharmāpi śabdo nityo ghaṭastvanityaḥ / kuta iti cet / sattvādisādharmye 'pi svabhāvaviśeṣasambhavāt / yathā dīpaḥ śabdo manuṣyo 'śva ityādi / iti sādharmyasamāśritamanumānamasiddham /
children.translated_text: If the wick is large, the flame is large; if the wick is small, the flame is also small—when this is established, the opponent says: if by common property, just as a pot and so on are impermanent, sound too would be so, then there would be a consequence of non-distinction of everything with everything. If you ask why: because of the common property of everything with everything. And what is this common property? It is said to be existence, oneness, and being an object of knowledge—this is called common property. If all things having common properties are different from particular things, then sound too is likewise. Even though sound has the common property of a pot and the like, sound is permanent while the pot is impermanent. If you ask why: because, even when there is common property such as existence, particular natures are possible. For example, a lamp, sound, a human, a horse, and so on. Thus the inference based on common property is unestablished.

body.translated_text: Sound is impermanent, because of the variation in its causes, sound varies—like a lamp.

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanaṃ kuta iti cet / sarveṣāṃ na mayā sattvādisādharmyaṃ pratiṣidvamapi tu teṣāṃ viśeṣa evāvadhāryate / sādharmyasampattitraividhyamanityatāṃ sthāpayati / taccāsmābhiranityatāsādhanāyocyate na tu sādharmyamātramupādīyate na khalvasti sā kāpi yuktiryā naivaṃ vicāryate / kasmāditi cet / naikamapi vidyate tādṛśaṃ yadanyavastuno na sadṛśaṃ na ca viśiṣṭaṃ syāt / tasmādyadi sādharmyamasti tadā tatsapakṣavarti sarvavipakṣavyāvṛttam / yadi tadupādānena hetusthāpanaṃ, siddho hetureṣa / sādharmyamātreṇa hetupratiṣṭhāpanaṃ tvasiddhaṃ tasmādviparītam /
body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. If you ask why: I have not denied the common property of existence and so on of all things, but rather I determine precisely their distinction. The threefold fulfillment of common property establishes impermanence. And that is stated by us for the purpose of proving impermanence—we do not merely adopt common property [alone]. Indeed, there is no reasoning that cannot be examined in this way. If you ask why: not a single thing exists that is not similar to some other thing and not distinct [from others]. Therefore, if there is common property, then it is present in the <s>sapakṣa</s> and excluded from all <s>vipakṣas</s>. If the reason is established by adopting that [common property], then this reason is proven. But establishment of a reason by common property alone is unproven—therefore [your refutation] is reversed.

body.text: punaścānityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvādghaṭavat / tasmācchabdo 'nityaḥ /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, sound is impermanent, because of being produced—like a pot. Therefore sound is impermanent.

body.text: prativādī prāha / hetuḥ pratijñā cābhāvānna bhidyete / ko nāmārtho hetusamutpādasya / hetvasaṃyoge śabdasyānutpāda (

children.text: ) iti / anutpannatvādabhāva evetyetasyārthaḥ / kathaṃ nāma śabdo 'nitya iti / anutpannaḥ śabda utpattimupalabhata utpanno vinaśyati / vināśāccābhāva evetyetasyārthaḥ / iti hetuḥ pratijñā cābhāvavat /
children.translated_text: this means: because it is not produced, it is simply non-existent. How can sound be impermanent? Sound, when not yet produced, obtains production; once produced, it perishes. And because of perishing, it is simply non-existent—this is the meaning. Thus the reason and the thesis are like non-existence.

body.translated_text: The opponent says: The reason and the thesis, due to non-existence, are not distinguished. What indeed is the purpose of producing a reason? Without the conjunction of the reason, sound is not produced—

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanam / kuta iti cet / asmatpratijñāyā abhāvaḥ pradhvaṃsābhāvātmakaḥ / asmatsthāpitahetorabhāvaḥ prāgabhāvaḥ / prāgabhāvaḥ sarvalokaprasiddhatvātsiddho 'nityatāhetutvena sthāpitaḥ / pradhvaṃsābhāvaḥ sāṃkhyādyaprasidvatvādasiddhaḥ / artho hi siddhena hetunā sthāpyate /
body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. If you ask why: the non-existence of our thesis is <s>pradhvaṃsābhāva</s> (destruction-non-existence, i.e., cessation). The non-existence of our established reason is <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior non-existence). <s>Prāgabhāva</s>, being universally acknowledged, is established as a reason for impermanence. <s>Pradhvaṃsābhāva</s>, not being accepted by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> and others, is unestablished. For a thesis is established by an established reason.

body.text: yadi siddhā pratijñopādīyate 'siddhastu heturbhavataḥ khaṇḍanasya viparyāso 'dhikataro bhavet / sarveṣāṃ vastūnāṃ pūrvamabhūtvā paścādabhāva iti mayoktam / tasmācchabdaḥ pūrvamasaṃścet paścādapyasan / yadi pūrvamasattvaṃ bhavato 'nanujñātaṃ tadaitadbhavatā cintyatām / yadi pūrvaṃ śabdaḥ sanneva na cāsti pratibandhastadā kasmācchrotreṇa nopalabhyate / tasmātpūrvamasattvaṃ nāgapadavaditi jñāyate / yadi kañcidviśiṣṭabuddhirabhimatamarthaṃ sādhayituṃ na śaknoti, iṣṭasādhanaṃ ca na yuktisampannaṃ so 'rtho nirasanīyaḥ /
body.translated_text: If an established thesis is adopted while the reason is unestablished, the reversal of your refutation would be even greater. What I have said is that all things, having previously not existed, subsequently cease to exist. Therefore, if sound previously did not exist, it also does not exist afterward. If the prior non-existence is not accepted by you, then consider this: if sound previously exists and there is no obstruction, then why is it not apprehended by the ear? Therefore, it is known that its prior non-existence is not like the footprint of a bird in the sky. If a certain special cognition cannot establish its intended object, and the means of establishing what is desired is not endowed with reasoning, then that object is to be rejected.

body.text: 5. prāptyaprāptikhaṇḍanam / hetuḥ sādhyaṃ prāpnoti na vā? / yadi tāvat sādhyaṃ prāpnoti tadāsādhakaḥ / atha hetuḥ sādhyaṃ na prāpnoti tadāpyasādhakaḥ / etatprāptyaprāptikhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 5. <s>Prāptyaprāptikhaṇḍana</s> (refutation by reaching and not-reaching). Does the reason reach the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) or not? If the reason reaches the <s>sādhya</s>, then it is inconclusive. If the reason does not reach the <s>sādhya</s>, then too it is inconclusive. This is called refutation by reaching and not-reaching.

body.text: prativādī prāha / yadi hetuḥ sādhyaṃ prāpnoti tadā sādhyena saṃsargātsādhyaṃ na sādhayati / yathā nadīvāri samudravāripraviṣṭaṃ na punarnadīvāri, hetustadvadasādhakaḥ / (

children.text: ) yadi sādhyamasiddhaṃ, tadā heturaprāpakaḥ / yadi prāpakastadā kiṃ siddhasyārthasya hetunā / tasmāddheturasiddhaḥ / atha na prāpnoti tadā so 'nyavastuvadasādhakaṃ, tasmaddheturasiddhaḥ / yadi heturaprāpakastadāsamarthaḥ / yathāgniraprāpya dahanāsamartho 'siścāprāpya chedanāsamarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: If the <s>sādhya</s> is unestablished, then the reason does not reach it. If it does reach, then what is the need of a reason for an already established object? Therefore, the reason is unestablished. If it does not reach, then like some other thing, it is inconclusive—therefore the reason is unestablished. If the reason does not reach, then it is incapable. Just as fire, without reaching, is incapable of burning, and a sword, without reaching, is incapable of cutting.

body.translated_text: The opponent says: if the reason reaches the <s>sādhya</s>, then due to its merger with the <s>sādhya</s>, it does not prove the <s>sādhya</s>. Just as river water that has entered ocean water is no longer river water—the reason, likewise, is inconclusive.

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanaṃ / dvividho hetuḥ / utpattiheturvyañjanahetuśca / yadi bhavataḥ khaṇḍanamutpattihetusamāśritaṃ tadā siddhaṃ khaṇḍanam / yadi vyañjanahetusamāśritaṃ tadā viparītam / kasmāditi cet / uktaṃ mayā yaddhetuḥ sādhyaṃ notpādayatyapi tu parapratipādanārthaṃ sādhyaṃ vyanaktyavyāvṛttatvāt / sādhyasattve 'pi sādhyasya yathārthajñānaṃ na jāyate / kuta iti cet / mohāt / tasmād vyañjanaheturityucyate / yathā rūpasattve 'pi pradīpaprayojanaṃ tadvyañjanārthaṃ na tu tadutpattyartham / tasmādvyañjanahetāvutpattikhaṇḍanaṃ viparītakhaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. The reason is twofold: a productive reason and a revealing reason. If your refutation relies on the productive reason, then the refutation is valid. If it relies on the revealing reason, then it is reversed. If you ask why: I have said that the reason does not produce the <s>sādhya</s>, but rather reveals the <s>sādhya</s> for the purpose of communicating it to others, due to its invariable concomitance. Even when the <s>sādhya</s> exists, correct knowledge of the <s>sādhya</s> does not arise. If you ask why: due to delusion. Therefore it is called a revealing reason. Just as even when a form exists, the purpose of a lamp is to reveal it, not to produce it. Therefore, applying the refutation of production to the revealing reason is a reversed refutation.

body.text: 6. ahetukhaṇḍanaṃ / traikālye hetorasambhava ityahetukhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 6. <s>Ahetukhaṇḍana</s> (refutation by absence of reason). The impossibility of the reason in all three times is called refutation by absence of reason.

body.text: prativādī prāha / kiṃ hetuḥ sādhyātpūrvaṃ paścādyugapadvā / yadi tāvaddhetuḥ prāk sādhyañca paścāttadāsati sādhye, hetuḥ kasya sādhakaḥ? / atha paścāt, sādhyañca prāk, tadā siddhe sādhye kiṃ hetunā? / atha yugapattadāhetuḥ / yathā yugapatsadbhāvāṅgoḥ śṛṅge dakṣiṇaṃ vāmaṃ vā parasparotpādake ityayuktam / tasmādyaugapadyañcettadā hetutvāsambhavaḥ /
body.translated_text: The opponent says: Is the reason prior to the <s>sādhya</s>, or subsequent, or simultaneous? If the reason is first and the <s>sādhya</s> afterward, then when the <s>sādhya</s> does not exist, what does the reason prove? If subsequent, and the <s>sādhya</s> is first, then when the <s>sādhya</s> is already established, what is the need for a reason? If simultaneous, then there is no reason. Just as, given the simultaneous existence of the two horns of a cow, the right and the left, it is improper [to say] that one produces the other. Therefore, if simultaneous, then the status of being a reason is impossible.

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanam / kuta iti cet / yatpūrvaṃ samutpannaṃ (

children.text: ) tadeva hetunā vyajyate yathā dīpaḥ vidyamānānyeva vastūni vyanakti na tvavidyamānāni vastūnyutpādayati / bhavān punarutpattihetunā me vyañjakahetuṃ khaṇḍayati tasmādviparītametatkhaṇḍanaṃ, na tu siddham /
children.translated_text: is itself revealed by the reason—just as a lamp reveals things that already exist but does not produce non-existent things. But you refute my revealing reason with [the logic of] a productive reason—therefore this refutation is reversed, not valid.

body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. If you ask why: that which has previously arisen

body.text: atha manyase yadyeṣa heturvyañjakaheturbhavati jñānābhāve sa kasya hetuḥ / tasmād vyañjakaheturasiddha iti kṛte khaṇḍane, tadā prāptikriyāsambhave heturnāma nopapadyate kriyāsadbhāve tu heturnāmopapadyate / yadā vyañjanakriyā tadaiva heturnāmopapadyate / taduktaṃ bhavati pūrvaṃ heturnāma nopapadyate paścāttu heturnāmopapadyate / yaccābhihitaṃ hetuḥ prāk kriyā tu paścāditi tadadoṣam / athaivaṃ sati, kriyāyā hetuto 'nutpattiriti cedetat khaṇḍanamasiddham / kasmāditi cet / etatprāgeva [sad] vastu paścāddheturnāmopapadyate / vastuni vinaṣṭe paścāt kriyotpattiriti cet, tadaitatkhaṇḍanaṃ sidhyati na tvevamucyate, pūrvaṃ bhāve 'pi [hetoriti] nāmānupapattiḥ paścāttu nāmopapattiḥ / tasmātphalasya hetuta utpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, if you think: if this reason is a revealing reason, in the absence of knowledge, whose reason is it? Therefore the revealing reason is unestablished—if such a refutation is made, then [I reply:] when the activity of reaching is impossible, the name 'reason' does not apply; but when activity exists, the name 'reason' does apply. When there is the activity of revealing, precisely then the name 'reason' applies. This amounts to saying: previously the name 'reason' does not apply, but subsequently the name 'reason' does apply. And what was said—that the reason comes first and the activity afterward—that is no fault. Now, if [you say] the activity does not arise from the reason—this refutation is unestablished. If you ask why: this very thing that [already] exists is subsequently given the name 'reason.' If you say that the thing is destroyed and the activity arises afterward, then this refutation would succeed—but it is not said thus. Previously, even while [the reason] exists, the name does not apply; subsequently, the name does apply. Therefore, the effect arises from the reason.

body.text: 7. upalabdhikhaṇḍanam / viśiṣṭahetunānityatāvarṇanādeṣo 'heturiti upalabdhikhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 7. <s>Upalabdhikhaṇḍana</s> (refutation by apprehension). Stating that through a distinguished reason the description of impermanence is not a [valid] reason—this is called refutation by apprehension.

body.text: prativādī prāha / yadi prayatna[ānantarīyaka]tvācchabdo 'nityastadā yatra prayatno na vidyate tatra nityatāprasaṅgaḥ / yathā vidyudvāyvādīnyaprayatna [ānantarīyaka]āṇyanityeṣu cāntarbhūtāni tasmādanityatve sādhye na prayatnamātraṃ samāśrayaṇīyaṃ prayatnasyāsādhanatvāt / sādhanañcedyatra yatra prayatno nāsti tatra tatra nityatāyāḥ sambhavaḥ / yathāgniṃ vinā na dhūmasthitiḥ / dhūmo 'gneḥ saddheturdhūmāgnyoravyatirekāt / (

children.translated_text: Tś 20

children.text: ) prayatnastu na tathā, tasmādasiddho hetuḥ / kiñca prayatno nānityatāsthāpanāsamarthaḥ / kuta iti cet / vyāptyabhāvāt / vyāptisambhave hyanityatāsthāpanopapattiḥ / vyāptyasambhave tvanityatāsthāpanānupapattiḥ / yathā kasyacitpratijñā syāt sarve taravo divyacetanā iti / kasmāditi cet / tarūṇāṃ nidrāsambhavācchirīṣavat / tatrāha khaṇḍayitā / tarūṇāṃ divyacetanāsiddhā / kasmāt? hetorvyāptyabhāvāt / śirīṣa eva svapiti na tvapare taravaḥ / sa svapno na sarvāṃstarūn vyāpnoti tasmātsarveṣāṃ tarūṇāṃ divyacetanatvapratiṣṭhāpane svapno 'samarthaḥ / prayatno 'pi tathā sarveṣāmanityānāmavyāpakatvādanityatāsthāpane 'samarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: ) But effort is not like that; therefore [effort] is an unestablished reason (<s>asiddha hetu</s>). Moreover, effort is incapable of establishing impermanence. If you ask why — because of the absence of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>). If pervasion is possible, then the establishment of impermanence is justified; but if pervasion is not possible, then the establishment of impermanence is not justified. For example, someone might have the thesis: 'All trees have divine consciousness.' If you ask why — because of the occurrence of sleep in trees, as in the <s>śirīṣa</s> tree. There the refuter says: the divine consciousness of trees is unestablished. Why? Because of the absence of pervasion of the reason. Only the <s>śirīṣa</s> tree sleeps, not other trees. That sleep does not pervade all trees; therefore sleep is incapable of establishing divine consciousness for all trees. Effort likewise, not pervading all impermanent things, is incapable of establishing impermanence.

body.translated_text: The respondent (<s>prativādin</s>) says: If sound is impermanent because it is a product of effort (<s>prayatna</s>), then where there is no effort, there would follow permanence. For instance, lightning, wind, and the like, which are not products of effort and are included among impermanent things — therefore, in proving impermanence, effort alone should not be relied upon, because effort is not a [universal] proof. And if it is a proof, then wherever effort does not exist, permanence would be possible. Just as without fire there is no existence of smoke — smoke is a valid reason (<s>saddhetu</s>) for fire, because of the non-deviation of smoke and fire. (

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanam / mayaivaṃ noktam / naitaducyate mayā yatprayatnaḥ sarvānityatākhyāpane samartho heturanye tu hetavo 'samarthāḥ / yadyanyo 'nityatākhyāpane samartho heturvidyate tadāhaṃ sukhī / asmadarthasiddheḥ / asmatsthāpito hetuḥ khyāpanasamarthaḥ, anyo 'pi hetuḥ khyāpanasamarthaḥ / tasmātpratijñā siddhā / yathā dhūmenāgniranumitaḥ / yadi kaścidvadetprabhayāgnirapi siddho 'smadarthe 'pi tathāsambhavaḥ / prayatnotpattiranityatākhyāpanasamarthā / yadyanye 'pi hetavo 'nityatākhyāpanasamarthā, anityatāpi siddhā / tasmādviparītaṃ khaṇḍanaṃ bhavataḥ / asmanmatākhaṇḍanāt / yadyahaṃ bravīmi yadyadanityaṃ tattatsarvaṃ prayatnasamutpannamiti tadā prayatnotpattihetoravyāpitvādasiddhatvamiti bhavatā khaṇḍanaṃ vaktavyam / tadaitacca khaṇḍanaṃ viśiṣyate / yadāhaṃ bravīmi śabdābikamanityaṃ prayatnasamutpannatvāttadā yatsarvamanityaṃ (

children.translated_text: Tś 21
) is all produced from effort' is not being made. Therefore your refutation is reversed.

body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed (<s>viparīta</s>). By me it was not stated thus — I do not say that effort is a reason capable of announcing all impermanence while other reasons are incapable. If there exists another reason capable of announcing impermanence, then I am satisfied, since our purpose is accomplished. The reason established by us is capable of announcement; another reason too is capable of announcement — therefore the thesis is established. Just as fire is inferred from smoke — if someone were to say 'fire is also established through [its] radiance,' the same possibility applies for our purpose too. The arising of effort is capable of announcing impermanence. If other reasons too are capable of announcing impermanence, then impermanence is indeed established. Therefore your refutation is reversed — because it does not refute our position. If I were to say 'whatever is impermanent, all of that is produced from effort,' then the refutation of the unpervasiveness of the reason of effort-production would be proper for you to state, and then that refutation would prevail. But when I say 'sound is impermanent because of being produced from effort,' the statement 'whatever is impermanent (

body.text: 8. saṃśayakhaṇḍanam / vipakṣasādharmyātsaṃśayavādena khaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: 8. Refutation by doubt (<s>saṃśayakhaṇḍana</s>). Refutation through the argument of doubt based on similarity with the counter-example (<s>vipakṣa</s>).

body.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnasamutpannatvāt / yadyatprayatnasamutpannaṃ tattadanityaṃ ghaṭavat / iti sthāpite prativādī prāha / yatsamutpannaṃ tatprayatena vyaktaṃ yathā mūlakīlakodakaṃ prayatnena vyaktaṃ na tu prayatnena samutpannam / śabdo 'pi tathā / tasmātprayatnadvārā hetusthāpanamaniyatamanutpanna utpanne ca bhāvāt / tasmāt taṃ hetumāśritya śabde saṃśayotpattiḥ / kathaṃ ca śabdo 'vadhāryate? kiṃ ghatavadasamutpannaḥ samutpadyate mūlakīlodakavatsamutpanno vā vyajyate? tasmadanaikāntikatā / tasmādutpattihetoḥ saṃśayotpādakatvādasādhakatvamiti jñeyam / kasmāt / utpādakatvād vyaktīkaraṇācca /
body.translated_text: Sound is impermanent, because of being produced from effort. Whatever is produced from effort is impermanent, like a pot. When this is established, the respondent says: What is produced may be merely manifested (<s>vyakta</s>) by effort — just as subterranean water at the base of a stake is manifested by effort but not produced by effort. Sound is likewise. Therefore, the establishment of the reason through effort is indeterminate, since [effort] is present in both the unproduced and the produced. Therefore, relying on that reason, doubt arises regarding sound. How is sound to be determined? Is it, like a pot, produced [when previously] non-existent? Or is it, like subterranean water [accessed by] a stake, manifested [when already] existent? Therefore, there is inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatā</s>). Therefore, because the reason of production generates doubt, it should be known to be non-probative. Why? Because of [the dual possibility of] production and manifestation.

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanam / kuta iti cet / noktamasmābhiryacchabdaḥ prayatnena vyaktaḥ / api tu yataḥ prayatnena samutpannastasmācchabdo 'nitya iti / punarbhavatā kiṃ khaṇḍyate / yadi (bhavato)cyate prayatnakāryaṃ dvividhamutpattirabhivyaktiśca / utpattirghaṭādivadabhivyaktirmūlakīlo dakādivat / śabdo 'pi prayatnakāryaḥ / tasmāttasmin nityatānityatāsaṃśayotpattiriti / tadayuktam / kuta iti cet / mūlakīlodakāderaprayatnakāryatvāt / mūlakīlodakābhivyaktiḥ prayatnakāryyeti cet / etadasmanmataṃ na khaṇḍayati / abhivyaktiranutpannā prayatnenotpatti labhate / tasmātprayatnakāryamekavidhaṃ sadaivanityatvāditi bhavatkhaṇḍanamayuktam / (

children.translated_text: Tś 22

children.text: ) atha manyase yatprayatna-[kāryaṃ] taddvidham / anityaṃ nityañca / ghaṭotpattiranityā ghaṭadhvaṃso nityaḥ / śabdo 'pi tatheti / eṣa saṃśayo 'yuktaḥ / kasmāt? asiddhatvāt / yadi bhavato ghaṭadhvaṃsasya dhvaṃse sadbhāvastataḥ sadbhāvāddhvaṃsābhāvaḥ syāt / yadi dhvaṃse 'bhāvastadā dhvaṃso 'bhāva eva / kuta iti cet / bhāvābhāvāt / andhakāravat / andhakāre jyotiṣo 'bhāvaḥ tasmādandhakāraḥ / dhvaṃso 'pi tathā / dhvaṃse bhāvābhāvaḥ tasmāddhvaṃsabhāva iti cet / tadayuktaṃ khapuṣpabandhyāputraśaśaviṣāṇeṣu bhāvābhāvātteṣāmapi sadbhāvaprasaṅgaḥ / yadi khapuṣpādīnāṃ sadbhāvo bhavatā nānujñāyate, tadā ghaṭadhvaṃsasyāpi tathātvam / tasmātsadbhāva iti na vaktavyam / tasmātprayatnakāryamekavidhaṃ sadaivānityatvāt / tasmādayukto bhavataḥ saṃśayaḥ / apratipattiścedbhavataḥ pratipādanārthamahaṃ vyañjanahetuṃ vadāmi / anityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt / prāgvyavadhānābhāvātprayatnenotpattiniṣpattiḥ / tasmādanityaḥ śabdo ghaṭavaditi jñātam / yatprayatnenopalabhyate yacca prayatnena kriyate tadubhayaṃ bhinnamiti bhavatā pratiṣṭhāpitam / tadayuktam / ko 'yamartho yatprayatnenopalabhyate tadanityamiti / kasmāt / yasmādanutpannaṃ samutpadyate samutpannañca vinaśyati / tasmānmūlakīlodakādestathāpyanityatāsambhavaḥ / yaccocyate yadabhivyaktaṃ nityamiti tasya kiṃ prayojanam /
children.translated_text: ) Now, if you think that the effect of effort is twofold — impermanent and permanent; the production of a pot is impermanent but the destruction of a pot is permanent; and sound is likewise — this doubt is unjustified. Why? Because it is unestablished. If the destruction of a pot, according to you, has [positive] existence within destruction, then from that existence there would be absence of destruction. If there is no existence within destruction, then destruction is simply non-existence. If you ask why — because of the absence of [positive] being. Like darkness: in darkness there is the absence of light, therefore [there is] darkness. Destruction is likewise. If you say 'in destruction there is the absence of [positive] being, therefore destruction is [a positive] being' — that is unjustified, for there would follow the positive existence of sky-flowers, barren women's sons, and hare's horns too, since in them too there is the absence of [positive] being. If the positive existence of sky-flowers and the like is not accepted by you, then the same applies to the destruction of a pot. Therefore, it should not be said to have positive existence. Therefore, the effect of effort is of one kind only, being always impermanent. Therefore your doubt is unjustified. If you lack understanding, I state a distinguishing reason for your comprehension: sound is impermanent. Why? Because, there being no prior obstruction, production is accomplished through effort. Therefore sound is impermanent, like a pot — this is understood. What you have established — that what is apprehended through effort and what is produced by effort are two different things — that is unjustified. What is the meaning of 'what is apprehended through effort is impermanent'? Why? Because what was unproduced comes into being, and what has come into being perishes. Therefore, even for subterranean water at a stake and the like, impermanence is [the case]. And as for what is said — 'what is manifested is permanent' — what is the purpose of that?

body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. If you ask why — it was not stated by us that sound is manifested by effort. Rather, because it is produced by effort, therefore sound is impermanent. Furthermore, what is being refuted by you? If you say that the effect of effort is twofold — production and manifestation; production is like a pot, manifestation is like subterranean water at a stake; and sound too is an effect of effort, therefore doubt arises in it regarding permanence and impermanence — that is unjustified. If you ask why — because subterranean water at a stake and the like are not effects of effort. If you say the manifestation of subterranean water at a stake is an effect of effort — this does not refute our position. The manifestation, [previously] unproduced, obtains production through effort. Therefore, the effect of effort is of one kind only, being always impermanent. Thus your refutation is unjustified. (

body.text: 9. anuktikhaṇḍanam / pūrvamanuktatvādanityatābhāva etadanuktikhaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: 9. Refutation by non-statement (<s>anuktikhaṇḍana</s>). Because [the reason for impermanence] was not previously stated, impermanence does not hold — this is the refutation by non-statement.

body.text: pratijñā pūrvavat / prativādī prāha / prayatna iti vacanaṃ śabdasyānityatāheturiti cettadā kiṃ prāpyate? (

children.translated_text: Tś 23

children.text: ) prayatna ityanukte tadā śabdo nityaḥ / etadeva prāpyate, pūrvakāle nitye sati kathamadhunānityaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: ) When 'effort' was not stated, then sound was permanent — this is precisely what is obtained. Since it was permanent at the prior time, how can it now be impermanent?

body.translated_text: The thesis is as before. The respondent says: If you claim that the word 'effort' is the reason for the impermanence of sound, then what is obtained? (

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanam / kasmāt / asmābhiḥ sthāpito heturabhivyaktyartho notpattyartho na vā vināśārthaḥ / yadyasmatsthāpitasya hetorvināśaḥ syāttadā bhavatkhaṇḍanaṃ viśiṣyeta / yadā heturmayānuktastadā śabdasyānityatānabhivyakteti cedbhavatkhaṇḍanam / etatkhaṇḍanābhāsa eva / yadi vināśahetunā mām khaṇḍayati bhavān tadviparītakhaṇḍanaṃ syāt /
body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. Why? The reason established by us is for the purpose of manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>), not for the purpose of production, nor for the purpose of destruction. If the destruction of our established reason were to occur, then your refutation would prevail. If, when the reason is not stated by me, you say 'the impermanence of sound is not manifested' — [this would be] your refutation. But this is merely an appearance of refutation. If you refute me with the cause of destruction, that would be a reversed refutation.

body.text: 10. kāryabhedakhaṇḍanam- kāryyabhedād ghaṭavatacchabda iti na vaktavyam / etat kāryabhedakhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 10. Refutation by difference of effect (<s>kāryabhedakhaṇḍana</s>) — Because of the difference of effect, it should not be said that sound is like a pot. This is called the refutation by difference of effect.

body.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvād ghaṭavaditi sthāpite prativādī prāha ghaṭaśabdayoḥ kāryabhedaḥ / kāryabhedāt tulyānityatānupapattiḥ /
body.translated_text: When [the thesis] is established that sound is impermanent because of being produced, like a pot, the respondent says: there is a difference of effect between a pot and sound. Because of the difference of effect, equal impermanence is unjustified.

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇdanam / kasmāt? / anitya śabdo ghaṭasamānakāryatvāditi noktaṃ mayā / api tu sarvāṇi vastūni tulyena nyāyena kṛtakatvād anityānītyevamuktam / na tu samānakāryāpekṣatvād ghaṭavacchabdo 'nitya iti / dhūmo bhinno 'pyagnivyañjakaḥ / ghaṭo 'pi tathā śabdasyanityatāvyañjakaḥ /
body.translated_text: This refutation is reversed. Why? It was not stated by me that sound is impermanent because of having the same effect as a pot. Rather, it was stated thus: all things, by equal reasoning, are impermanent because of being produced. Not that sound is impermanent like a pot because of having the same effect. Smoke, though different [from fire], is an indicator of fire. Likewise, a pot, [though different from sound], is an indicator of the impermanence of sound.

body.text: anyacca paraṇoktaṃ kāryaviśeṣakhaṇḍanam / anyadasti yenocyate nityaḥ śabda ākāśasamāśritatvāt / ākāśo nityaḥ / yatkiñcidākāśasamāśritaṃ tannityam / yathā paramāṇoḥ pārimāṇḍalyam / paramāṇurnityaḥ pārimāṇḍalyañca paramāṇusamāśritaṃ, tasmātpārimāṇḍalyaṃ nityam / śabdo 'pi tadvadākāśasamāśritatvānnityaḥ / anyacca / nityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt / śrāvaṇatvāt / yathā śabdatvaṃ (

children.translated_text: Tś 24

children.text: ) śravaṇagrāhyaṃ nityañca, tathā śabdo 'pi tasmānnityaḥ / etatpratijñāntaram /
children.translated_text: ) is apprehensible by hearing and is permanent, so too is sound; therefore it is permanent.' This is a different thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>).

body.translated_text: Furthermore, there is the refutation of a particular effect (<s>kāryaviśeṣakhaṇḍana</s>) stated by the opponent. Another [argument] by which it is said: 'Sound is permanent, because of being located in space (<s>ākāśa</s>). Space is permanent. Whatever is located in space is permanent. Just as the spherical nature (<s>pārimāṇḍalya</s>) of an atom. The atom is permanent, and sphericality is located in the atom; therefore sphericality is permanent. Sound, likewise, being located in space, is permanent.' And another [argument]: 'Sound is permanent. Why? Because of being audible (<s>śrāvaṇatva</s>). Just as the universal of sound-ness (

body.text: vaiśeṣika āha / yadi nityaṃ hetunā sthāpyate, tato hetukriyatvādanityam / tasmācchabdo 'nityaḥ /
body.translated_text: The <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> says: 'If permanence is established by a reason (<s>hetu</s>), then because of being an effect of a cause, it is impermanent. Therefore sound is impermanent.'

body.text: viparītametatkhaṇḍanam / kasmāt? na mayoktaṃ hetunā nityatotpanneti, api tu heturanityatāṃ vyanakti / parasyājñānātparasya pratipādanārthamasmatsthāpitaheturvyañjanaheturna tvutpattihetuḥ / bhavatkhaṇḍanamutpattihetoreva / tasmādviparītam /
body.translated_text: This is a contrary refutation (<s>viparītakhaṇḍana</s>). Why? I have not said that permanence is produced by a reason; rather, the reason manifests impermanence. Due to the other party's ignorance, the reason established by us is for the purpose of making the other understand—it is a reason for manifestation (<s>vyañjanahethu</s>), not a reason for production (<s>utpattihethu</s>). Your refutation [applies] only to a production-reason. Therefore it is contrary.

body.text: kiñca pratijñākhaṇḍane bhavadukte na mayānujñāte / kuta iti cet / nāsmābhiranityateṣṭā pratītā vā / tasmādukto mayaiṣo 'rthaḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, regarding the refutation of [my] thesis that you have stated—I do not accept [it]. If you ask why: impermanence is not accepted or acknowledged by us. Therefore this meaning has been stated by me.

body.text: etaddaśavidhaṃ viparītakhaṇḍanamucyate / viparyayeṇa taddoṣasthāpanāt / yadi khaṇḍanaṃ tattulyaṃ bhavettadā viparītakhaṇḍanāpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: This tenfold contrary refutation (<s>viparītakhaṇḍana</s>) is described. [It is called contrary] because of establishing the opponent's fault in a reverse manner. If the refutation is equivalent [to the thesis], then there is an incurrence of contrary refutation.

body.text: aparamasatkhaṇḍanam / mithyāvacanādasat / mithyāvacanaṃ tvayathārthamanarthakañca / etaducyate 'satkhaṇḍanam / asatkhaṇḍanaṃ trividhamavarṇya(vyañjaka) khaṇḍanamarthāpatti(vyañjaka)khaṇḍanaṃ, pratidṛṣṭa(ārthavyañjaka)khaṇḍanañca /
body.translated_text: Next, false refutation (<s>asatkhaṇḍana</s>). It is false because of being a wrong statement. A wrong statement is one that is not in accordance with the meaning and is meaningless. This is called false refutation. False refutation is threefold: refutation by non-descriptive indication (<s>avarṇyavyañjaka khaṇḍana</s>), refutation by presumptive indication (<s>arthāpattivyañjaka khaṇḍana</s>), and refutation by counter-example indication (<s>pratidṛṣṭārthavyañjaka khaṇḍana</s>).

body.text: 1. avarṇya(vyañjaka)khaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: 1. Refutation by non-descriptive indication (<s>avarṇyakhaṇḍana</s>).

body.text: pratyakṣaviṣaye yaddhetvanveṣaṇaṃ tadavarṇyakhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: The seeking of a reason (<s>hetu</s>) in a matter that is [established by] direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>)—this is called refutation by non-description.

body.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ / kuta iti cet / kṛtrimatvādghaṭavaditi sthāpite prativādī prāha / asmābhirdṛṣṭaṃ yadghaṭaḥ kṛtrimaḥ / kena hetunā tadanityatānumīyate / yadi hetuṃ vinā (
