children.translated_text: Tś 25

children.text: ) ghaṭasya nityatā sthāpitā śabdo 'pi nityetāhetumantareṇa nityo bhavet /
children.translated_text: ) the permanence of a pot is established, then sound too would be permanent without a reason.'

body.translated_text: 'Sound is impermanent. Why? Because of being produced, like a pot'—when this is established, the opponent says: 'We have seen that a pot is produced. By what reason is its impermanence inferred? If without a reason (

body.text: asattatkhaṇḍanam / kasmāt? / yat[pūrvameva]pratītaṃ na tasya hetunā sādhanam / yadi pratīyate yadvaṭaḥ sahetuko 'nityaśceti kimanityatāhetvanmveṣaṇena / tasmādasadetatkhaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: This is a false refutation. Why? For what is already apprehended [through perception], there is no need for establishment by a reason. If it is apprehended that a pot is produced from a cause and is impermanent, then what is the need for seeking a reason for impermanence? Therefore this refutation is false.

body.text: 2. arthāpatti(vyañjaka)khaṇḍanam / vipakṣe 'rthāpattiretadarthāpattikhaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: 2. Refutation by presumption (<s>arthāpattikhaṇḍana</s>). A presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) regarding the counter-thesis—this is refutation by presumption.

body.text: ātmā na vidyate / kuta iti cet / anabhivyaktatvādvandhyāputravaditi sthāpite prativādī prāha / tadetadarthādāpattiryadyabhivyaktaṃ sadanabhivyaktaṃ tvasaditi / athābhivyaktaṃ kadācitsatkadācidasa / anabhivyaktaṃ tadvat / alātacakramarīcigandharvanagaravat / tadabhivyaktam / tatsadbhāvasthāpanaṃ tvaśakyam / yadyabhivyaktasya sadbhāvasthāpanamaśakyaṃ tadānabhivyaktasyāsadbhāvapratiṣṭhāpanaṃ [sutarāma] śakyam /
body.translated_text: 'The self (<s>ātman</s>) does not exist. Why? Because of being unmanifested, like the son of a barren woman'—when this is established, the opponent says: 'This is a presumption from the meaning: what is manifested exists, and what is unmanifested does not exist.' But what is manifested is sometimes existent and sometimes non-existent. The unmanifested is likewise. Like a whirling firebrand circle, a mirage, or a <s>gandharva</s> city (city of illusions)—these are manifested. But establishing their real existence is impossible. If establishing the real existence of what is manifested is impossible, then establishing the non-existence of what is unmanifested is [all the more] possible.'

body.text: asattatkhaṇḍanam / ko 'sau nyāyo yenaitadarthādāpattirbhavet / yadanabhivyaktaṃ tadatyantamasaditi naitadarthādāpadyate / abhivyaktaṃ dvividhamanarthāpattirarthāpattiśca / yadi vṛṣṭirbhavati tadā meghenāpi bhavitavyam / meghe satyapi tu kadācidṛṣṭirbhavati kadācinna bhavatītyanaikāntikatā / dhūmenāgneranumānam / nātrārthādāpattiḥ / dhūme dṛṣṭe satyagniranumīyate dhūme tvasati agnerabhāvaḥ / anarthāpattiriyam / kasmāditi cet / taptāyaḥpiṇḍe lohitāṅgāre ca dhūmābhāve 'pya 'gneḥ sadbhāvaḥ / tasmādabhivyakteṣvarthāpattikhaṇḍanamabhūtam /
body.translated_text: This is a false refutation. What reasoning is there by which this would be a presumption from the meaning? That what is unmanifested is absolutely non-existent—this does not follow from the meaning. The manifested is of two kinds: non-presumption and presumption. If there is rain, then there must also be a cloud. But even when there is a cloud, sometimes there is rain and sometimes not—so this is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). Inference of fire from smoke: this is not a presumption from meaning. When smoke is seen, fire is inferred; but in the absence of smoke, fire is absent. This is non-presumption (<s>anarthāpatti</s>). Why? Because even in a heated iron ball or a glowing coal, though there is no smoke, fire exists. Therefore, the presumption-based refutation regarding manifested things is unfounded.

body.text: anyacca / rūpamevālātacakramarīcigandharvanagarāṇīti pratibhātīndriyabhramāccittaviparyāsena / tacca vartamāna eva (

children.translated_text: Tś 26

children.text: ) sadanāgate tvasat / rūpamātramindriyabhramāccittaviparyāsena kadācit sad[vastīva] prakāśate / yaduktaṃ bhavatābhivyaktasya sattvamanaikāntikaṃ tadayuktam / kiñca bandhyāputradṛṣṭāntenāyamevārtho mayā niścīyate / yadabhivyaktisthānānna prabhraṃśate tadvastvabhāva eva / bandhyāutravat / yaccānabhivyaktisthānātprabhraṃśate naiṣo me dṛṣṭāntaḥ / aṇvākāśādiṣu tu kadācidabhivyaktiḥ kadācidanabhivyaktiḥ / bhavadarthāpattiḥ prati mayārthāpattiruktā / yadabhivyaktisthānādekāntena prabhraṃśate tadvastu sadeva / alātacakrādiṣu cakramevānaikāntikam / tacca cakrasyānaikāntikatā yat pravartanakāle sat, sthitikāle cāsat / tasmāt neyamarthāpattiḥ / anarthāpattāvarthāpattikhaṇḍanaṃ cedetat khaṇḍanamasat / punaranyathāpyarthāpattikhaṇḍanaṃ vadanti / yadi ghaṭasādharmyādanityaḥ śabda ityarthādāpannaṃ tadāsādharmyānnityaḥ / asādharmyaṃ yacchabdaḥ śravaṇagrāhyo 'mūrtaśca ghaṭastu cakṣurgrāhyo mūrtaśca / asādharmyācchabdo nityaḥ /
children.translated_text: ) exists in the present, but does not exist in the future. A mere form, through sensory error and mental misapprehension, sometimes appears as if [really] existing. What you have said—that the existence of the manifested is inconclusive—that is improper. Moreover, by the example of the son of a barren woman, this very meaning is ascertained by me: what does not deviate from the state of non-manifestation is indeed the absence of a real entity—like the son of a barren woman. And what deviates from the state of non-manifestation—that is not my example. But in the case of atoms, space, and the like, there is sometimes manifestation and sometimes non-manifestation. Against your presumption, I have stated a [counter-]presumption: what exclusively deviates from the state of manifestation is indeed a real entity. In the case of the whirling firebrand and the like, the circle itself is inconclusive—and the inconclusiveness of the circle is that it exists at the time of revolving and does not exist at the time of rest. Therefore this is not a [valid] presumption. If this refutation amounts to applying a presumption-refutation where there is non-presumption, then this refutation is false. Furthermore, others state a presumption-refutation in yet another way: 'If sound is impermanent because of similarity with a pot, then by presumption from dissimilarity, it is permanent. The dissimilarity is: sound is apprehensible by hearing and is formless, while a pot is apprehensible by sight and has form. Because of dissimilarity, sound is permanent.'

body.translated_text: Furthermore, the whirling firebrand circle, mirage, and <s>gandharva</s> city—these appear as forms due to sensory error and mental misapprehension. And that [appearance] (

body.text: evaṃvidhakhaṇḍanaṃ sādharmyakhaṇḍanato 'rthāpattikhaṇḍanāviśeṣānna mayānujñātam /
body.translated_text: Such a refutation is not accepted by me, because there is no difference between a refutation based on similarity and a refutation based on presumption.

body.text: 3. pratidṛṣṭāntakhaṇḍanam / pratidṛṣṭāntabalāt sādhanam / etaducyate pratidṛṣṭānta (vyañjaka) khaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: 3. Refutation by counter-example (<s>pratidṛṣṭāntakhaṇḍana</s>). Proof by the force of a counter-example—this is called refutation by counter-example.

body.text: anityaḥ śabdo 'nityaghaṭasādharmyāditi cet / tadāhamapi tasya nityatāṃ vyaktīkaromi / yathā nityākāśasādharmyānnityaḥ śabdaḥ / yadi nityatāsādharmyānnityatāprāptistadānityatāsādharmyātkathamanityatā /
body.translated_text: 'Sound is impermanent because of similarity with an impermanent pot'—if [this is stated], then I too demonstrate its permanence: 'Sound is permanent because of similarity with permanent space.' If permanence is obtained through similarity with [something] permanent, then how can impermanence [be obtained] through similarity with [something] impermanent?

body.text: asattatkhaṇḍanam / kuta iti cet / abhāvamātra vastvākāśamucyate / (

children.translated_text: Tś 27

children.text: ) yadi sato nityavaṃ siddhastadā dṛṣṭāntaḥ sada khaṇḍanam / kintvatrāmato nityatā / ākāśamasadvastvera naitannityamanityaṃ vā vaktuṃ śakyate / asiddho dṛṣṭānta etasya khaṇḍanasya / adṛṣṭānte dṛṣṭāntatākalpanāt / tasmādasadetatkhaṇḍanam / yadi kaścinmanyate sadvastvevākāśo nityaśca / etadviparītakhaṇḍanaṃ natu satkhaṇḍanam / kasmāt? / amūrtatvasyanaikāntikatvāt / ākāśo 'mūrto nityaśca cittasukhaduḥkhecchādikantvamūrtamanityam / amūrtaḥ śabdaḥ kimākāśavannityo bhaveccittasukhādivadanityo vā / amūrtatvamanaikāntikatvādasiddho hetuḥ / tasmādviparītametkhaṇḍanam / aparaṃ ca sahetukatvācchabdo 'nityaḥ / vastu sahetukañcet tadānityamiti jñeyaṃ ghaṭādivaditi sthāpite / prativādī prāha / asminnarthe saṃśayaḥ / kasmāditi cet / ghaṭotpādaḥ sahetuko 'nityaḥ / ghaṭadhvaṃsastu sahetuko nityaḥ / śabdasya sahetukatvācchabde saṃśayotpattiḥ / sahetukaghaṭotpādavadanityaḥ sahetukaghaṭadhvaṃsavannityo vā /
children.translated_text: ) If permanence of an existent [entity] is established, then the example is sound and the refutation [stands]. But here [space's] permanence is not [of that kind]. Space is a non-existent entity—it cannot be said to be either permanent or impermanent. The example of this refutation is unestablished—because of fabricating an example where there is no [valid] example. Therefore this refutation is false. If someone thinks that space is indeed a real entity and is permanent, this is a contrary refutation, not a sound refutation. Why? Because formlessness (<s>amūrtatva</s>) is inconclusive. Space is formless and permanent, but mind, pleasure, pain, desire, and such are also formless yet impermanent. Is formless sound permanent like space, or impermanent like mind, pleasure, and such? Because formlessness is inconclusive, the reason is unestablished. Therefore this is a contrary refutation. Furthermore: 'Sound is impermanent because of having a cause. If a thing has a cause, it should be known as impermanent, like a pot and such'—when this is established, the opponent says: 'In this matter there is doubt. Why? The production of a pot has a cause and is impermanent. But the destruction of a pot also has a cause and is permanent. Because sound has a cause, doubt arises regarding sound—is it impermanent like the causally-produced pot, or permanent like the causally-produced destruction of a pot?'

body.translated_text: This is a false refutation. Why? Space is said to be a mere absence of a real entity. (

body.text: asadetkhaṇḍanam / kasmāt? yadyasaddravyaṃ nityamucyate daṇḍāghātavinaṣṭavastūnāmapi nityatāpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: This is a false refutation. Why? If a non-existent substance is said to be permanent, then even things destroyed by the blow of a stick would incur permanence.

body.text: kiñca śabdo 'nityaḥ / kutaḥ aindriyakatvāt / ghaṭādivaditi sthāpite / prativādī prāha / atrāpi saṃśayasambhavaḥ / yadyaindriyakaḥ sāmānyavattadā nityatāpattiḥ / yadi śabda aindriyakastadā sāmānyavannityaḥ / yadi sāmānyavanna nityo bhavet, tadā ghaṭadṛṣṭāntenānityo na bhavet /
body.translated_text: Furthermore: 'Sound is impermanent. Why? Because of being perceptible by the senses (<s>aindriyakatva</s>), like a pot and such'—when this is established, the opponent says: 'Here too doubt is possible. If it is perceptible by the senses like a universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), then permanence would follow. If sound is perceptible by the senses, then it is permanent like a universal. If a universal is not permanent, then by the pot example, [sound] would not be impermanent [either].'

body.text: asadetatkhaṇḍanam / kasmāt / yadi gavādisāmānyaṃ gavādivyatiriktaṃ syāttadā pṛthaktvena grāhyaṃ draṣṭavyañca (

children.translated_text: Tś 28

children.text: ) sāmānyantu gavādivyatiriktaṃ pṛthaktvena gṛhyate na ca dṛśyate / tasmādanityamiti jñeyam /
children.translated_text: ) But the universal, being separate from cows and such, is apprehended [only conceptually] but not seen [directly]. Therefore it should be known as impermanent.

body.translated_text: This is a false refutation. Why? If the universal of cow and such were separate from cows and such, then it should be apprehensible and visible as a separate [entity]. (

body.text: anyacca / ātmā na vidyate / kuta iti cet / anabhivyaktatvāt / sarpaśravaṇavat / iti sthāpite prativādī prāha / samudrabinduparimāṇaṃ himālayagurutvañca madeva kintvanabhivyakte / ātmano 'pi tathātvasambhavaḥ / sanneva kintvanabhivyaktaḥ / tasmādanabhivyaktiheturnātmābhāvaṃ sthāpayituṃ samarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the self (<s>ātman</s>) does not exist. If you ask why: because it is not manifest. Like a serpent [merely] heard of. When this is established, the opponent says: The measure of drops in the ocean and the weight of the <s>Himālaya</s> exist in me, but are not manifest. The same possibility applies to the self as well—it exists but is simply not manifest. Therefore, the reason of non-manifestation is not capable of establishing the non-existence of the self.

body.text: saṅkhyāparimāṇasya sañcitādapṛthaktvam / tatparimeyasañcitamanukrameṇeyaditīyaditi ca pradarśyate / tatsaṅkhyāparimāṇaṃ smṛtidhāraṇārthaṃ, ekaṃ, daśa, sahasraṃ niyutamityādyucyate / samudrabinduparimāṇasya himālayagurutvasya cāpṛthaktvena satvābhāvāt / yadyaparakhaṇḍanaṃ tatkhaṇḍanasadṛśaṃ taddoṣasthāpanādasatkhaṇḍanamityucyate /
body.translated_text: The totality of a countable measure is not separate from what is accumulated. That measurable accumulation is demonstrated progressively as "this much" and "this much." That numerical measure, for the purpose of memory and retention, is expressed as one, ten, thousand, ten-thousand, and so forth. Since the measure of drops in the ocean and the weight of the <s>Himālaya</s> do not exist separately [from their components]. If the refutation of another is similar to [one's own position being] refuted, then by establishing that fault, it is called an invalid refutation.

body.text: viruddhakhaṇḍanam / arthavisaṃvādakaṃ viruddhamityucyate, yathā prabhāndhakārau sthitigatī visaṃvādake / tadviruddhakhaṇḍanamityucyate /
body.translated_text: Contradictory refutation (<s>viruddhakhaṇḍana</s>). That which is inconsistent with the meaning is called contradictory, just as light and darkness, or standing and going, are inconsistent. That is called contradictory refutation.

body.text: viruddhakhaṇḍanaṃ trividham / anutpattikhaṇḍanaṃ, nityatākhaṇḍanaṃ, svārthaviruddhakhaṇḍanañca /
body.translated_text: Contradictory refutation is of three kinds: refutation by non-origination (<s>anutpattikhaṇḍana</s>), refutation by permanence (<s>nityatākhaṇḍana</s>), and refutation contradicting one's own thesis (<s>svārthaviruddhakhaṇḍana</s>).

body.text: 1. athānutpattikhaṇḍanam / prāgutpatteḥ prayatnanirapekṣatvānnitya ityanutpattikhaṇḍanam /
body.translated_text: 1. Now, refutation by non-origination: "Prior to origination, because of not depending on effort, [sound] is permanent"—this is the refutation by non-origination.

body.text: prativādī prāha / yadyanityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatna[ānantarīyaka]tvāttadā prāgutpatteraprayatna[ānantarīyaka]tvānnityaḥ /
body.translated_text: The opponent says: If sound is impermanent because of being a product of effort, then prior to origination, because of not being a product of effort, it is permanent.

body.text: viruddhaṃ tatkhaṇḍanam / kuta iti cet / utpatteḥ pūrvaṃ śabdo 'sanneva / asaṃścet, kathaṃ nityaḥ / yadi kaścidvadedvandhyāputraḥ (

children.translated_text: (Tarkaśāstra 29)

children.text: ) kṛṣṇo bandhyāputraḥ śveta iti tadapi siddham bhavet / yadyasannityatānupapattiḥ / yadi nityo 'sattānupapattiḥ / asannityamiti svato viruddham / etadasatkhaṇḍaneṣvarthāpattisamam / kasmāt / asatkhaṇḍanāt / śabdo 'nityaḥ prayatna[ānantarīyakatvā]diti sthāpita etadarthādāpadyate / aprayatna[ānantarīya]katvānnitya iti tadasat / kutaḥ / prayatna[ānantarīya] kaṃ trividham, nityamanityamasacca / nityamākāśavat / anityaṃ vidyudādivat / asadākāśakusumāditiva / etatritayamaprayatna[ānantarīya] kaṃ bhavatā tvekena prakāreṇa nityamiti manyate / tasmādasat /
children.translated_text: is dark" or "the son of a barren woman is fair," that too would be established [by the same logic]. If non-existent, permanence is impossible. If permanent, non-existence is impossible. "Non-existent and permanent"—this is self-contradictory. This is equivalent to presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) among invalid refutations. Why? Because it is an invalid refutation. When it is established that "sound is impermanent because of being a product of effort," from the meaning of this it follows [that the opponent argues]: "because of not being a product of effort, it is permanent"—that is invalid. Why? That which is not a product of effort is of three kinds: permanent, impermanent, and non-existent. Permanent, like space. Impermanent, like lightning and the like. Non-existent, like a flower in the sky and the like. These three [kinds] are all not products of effort, but you consider [what is not a product of effort] to be permanent in only one way. Therefore, [your refutation] is invalid.

body.translated_text: That refutation is contradictory. If you ask why: prior to origination, sound simply does not exist. If non-existent, how can it be permanent? If someone were to say, "the son of a barren woman

body.text: 2. nityatākhaṇḍanam / nityamanityabhāvānnityaḥ śabdaḥ / etannityatākhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 2. Refutation by permanence: "Sound is permanent because impermanence has the nature of permanence." This is called refutation by permanence.

body.text: prativādī prāha / anitye nityamanityatā, sarvadharmāṇāṃ svabhāvānirāsāt / anitye nityamanityatvabhāvānnityatā siddhā /
body.translated_text: The opponent says: In what is impermanent, the impermanence is permanent, since the own-nature of all <s>dharmas</s> cannot be negated. Because the impermanence in what is impermanent has the nature of permanence, permanence is established.

body.text: viruddhametat / kasmāt / yadyanityaṃ nityatālābhaḥ katham / yadi kaścidvadedandhakāre prabhāstīti tadvacanamapi siddhaṃ bhavet / tannaiveti cettato bhavatkhaṇḍanamapi viruddhamasacca / kasmāditi cet / anityateti pṛthagdharmo 'nityena na sambaddhaḥ yo nityo mantavyaḥ / anityatā naiva pṛthagbhāvaḥ / yadyanutpannaṃ vastūtpattiṃ labhata utpannantu vinaśyati tato 'nityamityucyate / anityamasaditi cedyadanityena nityaṃ śthāpitaṃ tasyāpyasattāprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: This is contradictory. Why? If [something is] impermanent, how can it attain permanence? If someone were to say "in darkness there is light," that statement too would be established [by the same logic]. If [you say] that is not so, then your refutation too is contradictory and invalid. If you ask why: "impermanence" is not a separate attribute unconnected with the impermanent, which should be regarded as permanent. Impermanence is certainly not a separate entity. If an unarisen thing attains arising and what has arisen is destroyed, then it is called impermanent. If you say the impermanent is non-existent, then what was established as permanent by [arguing from] impermanence—its non-existence too would follow.

body.text: 3. svārthaviruddham / yadi parārthasvaṇḍane svārthahānistadā tatsvārthaviruddhakhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: 3. Contradiction of one's own thesis: If in refuting another's thesis one's own thesis is destroyed, that is called refutation contradicting one's own thesis (<s>svārthaviruddhakhaṇḍana</s>).

body.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvādaṅkurādivaditi sthāpite / prativādī prāha / yadi heturanityatāṃ prāpnoti tadānityatātulyaḥ / yadyanityatāṃ na prāpnoti tadānityatāsādhanāsamarthaḥ / tasmādasiddho heturiti /
body.translated_text: When it is established that "sound is impermanent because of being produced, like a sprout and the like," the opponent says: If the reason (<s>hetu</s>) attains impermanence, then it is equivalent to impermanence [and cannot prove it]. If it does not attain impermanence, then it is incapable of proving impermanence. Therefore the reason is unestablished.

body.text: yadi tāvattava khaṇḍanaṃ matpratijñāṃ prāpnoti, matpratijñātulyatve 'smadarthakhaṇḍanāsamartham / atha na matpratijñāṃ prāpnoti tathāpyasmadarthakhaṇḍanāsamartham / tasmādbhavatkhaṇḍane bhavadarthahāniḥ /
body.translated_text: If your refutation attains [the level of] my thesis, then being equivalent to my thesis, it is incapable of refuting my meaning. If it does not attain my thesis, even then it is incapable of refuting my meaning. Therefore, in your refutation, your own thesis is destroyed.

body.text: prativādī punarāha / yadi hetuḥ pūrvaṃ pratijñā tu paścāt, tadā pratijñābhāve sa kasya hetuḥ / atha pratijñā pūrvaṃ hetustu paścāttadā, siddhāyāṃ pratijñāyāṃ kiṃ hetunetyeṣo 'pyasiddho hetuḥ /
body.translated_text: The opponent says again: If the reason comes first and the thesis afterward, then in the absence of a thesis, of what is it the reason? If the thesis comes first and the reason afterward, then when the thesis is already established, what need is there of a reason? Thus this too is an unestablished reason.

body.text: yadi bhavatkhaṇḍanaṃ pūrvamasmatpratijñā tu paścādasmadarthābhāve kiṃ bhavatā khaṇḍyate / yadyasmatpratijñā pūrvaṃ bhavatkhaṇḍanaṃ tu paścāttadāsmatpratijñāyāṃ sthāpitāyāṃ kiṃ bhavatkhaṇḍanena / bhavānasmatkhaṇḍanānujñānādasmatkhaṇḍanopādānena mā khaṇḍayatīti cettadayuktam / kasmāditi cet / mayā prakaṭitaṃ yadbhavatkhaṇḍanaṃ bhavadarthameva pratiṣedhati na tu bhavatkhaṇḍanamavalambyāsmadartho pratiṣṭhāpitaḥ / aparakhaṇḍane tatkhaṇḍanatulye sati taddoṣapratiṣṭhāpanaṃ viruddhakhaṇḍanamucyate /
body.translated_text: If your refutation comes first and our thesis afterward, then in the absence of our meaning, what is being refuted by you? If our thesis comes first and your refutation comes afterward, then when our thesis is already established, what is the use of your refutation? If you say "I refute by adopting your refutation, by permission of your refutation"—that is unjustified. If you ask why: the refutation I have exposed refutes your own meaning; my meaning is not established by relying on your refutation. When a counter-refutation is similar to that refutation, establishing the fault of that [original refutation] is called contradictory refutation.

body.text: samyakkhaṇḍanaṃ pañcavidham / iṣṭārthadūṣaṇam, aniṣṭārthavyaktiḥ, prasaṅgavyaktiḥ, viṣamārthavyaktiḥ, marvānyāyasiddhilābhavyaktiḥ /
body.translated_text: Proper refutation (<s>samyakkhaṇḍana</s>) is fivefold: exposing the fault of the desired meaning (<s>iṣṭārthadūṣaṇa</s>), revealing an undesired consequence (<s>aniṣṭārthavyakti</s>), revealing an unintended implication (<s>prasaṅgavyakti</s>), revealing an inconsistency (<s>viṣamārthavyakti</s>), and revealing the attainment of establishing all [absurd] conclusions (<s>sarvānyāyasiddhilābhavyakti</s>).

body.text: prativādī prāha / astyātmā saṃghātasya parārthatvāt / (

children.translated_text: (Tarkaśāstra 31)

children.text: ) yathā śayanāsanādisaṃghātaḥ parārthaḥ / cakṣurādīndriyasaṃghāto 'pi parārthaḥ / parastvātmā / tasmādastyātmeti jñātam /
children.translated_text: Just as the aggregate of bed, seat, and the like serves another's purpose, so also the aggregate of sense organs such as the eye and the like serves another's purpose. That other is the self. Therefore it is known that the self exists.

body.translated_text: The opponent says: The self (<s>ātman</s>) exists, because the aggregate serves another's purpose.

body.text: nāstyātmā / kuta iti cet / ekāntānabhivyaktatvāt / yadekāntānabhivyaktaṃ tadasadeva / yathānīśvarapuruṣasya dvitīyo mūrdhā / dvitīyo mūrdhā rūpagandhādimūrdhākārato na pṛthak mantavyaḥ / tasmādasan / ātmano 'pi tathātvasambhavaḥ / cakṣurādīndriyeṣu na hi sa pṛthagabhivyaktaḥ / tasmādasan / astyātmeti cettadayuktam / tadiṣṭadūṣaṇamucyate /
body.translated_text: The self does not exist. If you ask why: because it is absolutely non-manifest. Whatever is absolutely non-manifest is non-existent—like a second head on a person who does not [have one]. A second head should not be regarded as separate from the first head in form, smell, and the shape of a head. Therefore it is non-existent. The same possibility applies to the self—it is not manifest as something separate in the sense organs such as the eye. Therefore it is non-existent. If you say the self exists, that is unjustified. This is called the exposure of the fault of the desired thesis (<s>iṣṭadūṣaṇa</s>).

body.text: yadi punarbhavān vadati yadātmalakṣaṇamaviśeṣyaṃ, sa tu sanniti tadā dvitīyo mūrdhaviśeṣyo 'pi sanneva bhavet / dvitīyo mūrdhā sanniti bhavatā cenna pratipādyate tadātmanyapi tathā pratipattavyam / iyamucyate 'niṣṭārthavyaktiḥ /
body.translated_text: If, moreover, you say that the characteristic of the self is indeterminate yet it exists, then a second head, which is also indeterminate, would also exist. If you [do] not maintain that a second head exists, then the same should be understood regarding the self. This is called the revelation of an undesired consequence (<s>aniṣṭārthavyakti</s>).

body.text: yadi bhavanmate ubhau tulyamevāviśeṣyau / nyāyāsamāśrayāccātmā sanna punardvitīyo mūrdhā / tadāhamapi nyāyāsamaśrayātsanneva dvitīyo mūrdhā na tvātmeti cedvadeyameṣo 'rthaḥ sidvo bhavet / athāsmadartho na siddho bhavadartho 'pi na sidva ityucyate prasaṅgavyaktiḥ /
body.translated_text: If, in your view, both are equally indeterminate—and the self exists because it rests upon reasoning, while the second head does not—then I too could say that, resting upon reasoning, the second head exists but not the self; and this meaning would be established. If our meaning is not established, your meaning too is not established. This is called the revelation of unintended implication (<s>prasaṅgavyakti</s>).

body.text: anyacca / ātmā dvitīya iva mūrdhāviśeṣyaḥ na tvasanniti cettadā vaiṣamyadoṣo bhavanmūrdhyāpatet / yadi kaścidvadedvandhyāputraḥ sālaṅkāro bandhyāputro niralaṅkāra iti tadapi siddhaṃ bhavet / yadi kaścidevaṃ vadettadā vaiṣamyadoṣāpattiḥ / bhavato 'pi tathātvasambhavaḥ / iyaṃ vaiṣamyadoṣavyaktiḥ / athocyate nyāyāsamāśrayānniyatamevāstyātmā, nyāyāsamāśrayānniyatameva nāsti dvitīyo mūrdheti siddhaṃ ca tadvacanamiti tadā (

children.translated_text: (Tarkaśāstra 32)

children.text: ) mūrkhabālānyāyavacanānyapi sidhyeyuryathākāśo dṛśyaḥ, śītolo 'gniḥ, grāhyoḥ vāyurityādi mūrkhavacanāninyāyāsamāśritānyapi bhavatsādhyavat siddhāni bhaveyuḥ / asiddhāni cedbhavadartho 'pyevaṃ syāt / iyamucyate sarvānyāyasiddhilābhavyaktiḥ //
children.translated_text: the statements of fools and children, which are contrary to reason, would also be established—such as "space is visible," "fire is cool," "wind is graspable," and the like. These foolish statements, though lacking in reason, would be established just like your proposition. If they are not established, then your meaning would be the same. This is called the revelation of the attainment of establishing all [absurd] conclusions (<s>sarvānyāyasiddhilābhavyakti</s>).

body.translated_text: Furthermore, if [you say] the self, like the second head, is indeterminate but not non-existent, then the fault of inconsistency (<s>vaiṣamya</s>) would fall upon you regarding the [second] head. If someone were to say "the son of a barren woman is adorned" and "the son of a barren woman is unadorned," that too would be established [by the same logic]. If someone says thus, then the fault of inconsistency arises. The same possibility applies to you. This is the revelation of the fault of inconsistency (<s>viṣamārthavyakti</s>). If, however, you say: "Because it rests upon reasoning, the self definitely exists; because it rests upon reasoning, the second head definitely does not exist"—and this statement is established—then

body.text: iti dvitīyaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: Thus ends the second chapter.

body.text: atha tṛtīyaṃ prakaraṇam /
body.translated_text: Now, the third chapter.

body.text: dvāviṃśatividhā nigrahasthānāpattiḥ / 1 pratijñāhāniḥ, 2 pratijñāntaram, 3 pratijñāvirodha, 4 pratijñāsaṃnyāsaḥ, 5 hetvantaram, 6 arthāntaram, 7 nirarthakam, 8 avijñātārtham, 9 apārthakam, 10 aprāptakālaṃ, 11 nyūnam, 12 adhikam, 13 punaruktam, 14 ananubhāṣaṇam, 15 ajñānam, 16 apratibhā, 17 vikṣepaḥ (vyājairdūṣaṇaparihāraḥ) 18 matānujñā (paradūṣaṇānujñā), 19 paryanuyojyopekṣaṇam (nigrahasthānaprāptasya nigrahasthānāpattyupekṣaṇam), 20 niranuyojyānuyogaḥ (asthāne nigrahasthānābhiyogaḥ), 21 apasiddhāntaḥ, 22 hetvābhāsāśceti dvāviṃśatibidhāni nigrahasthānāni / yadi kasyacinnigrahasthānāpattirbhavet, na punastena saha vādaḥ kartavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: The incurrence of a point of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>) is of twenty-two kinds: (1) abandonment of the thesis (<s>pratijñāhāni</s>), (2) shifting the thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>), (3) contradiction of the thesis (<s>pratijñāvirodha</s>), (4) renunciation of the thesis (<s>pratijñāsaṃnyāsa</s>), (5) shifting the reason (<s>hetvantara</s>), (6) irrelevant meaning (<s>arthāntara</s>), (7) meaninglessness (<s>nirarthaka</s>), (8) unintelligible meaning (<s>avijñātārtha</s>), (9) incoherence (<s>apārthaka</s>), (10) untimeliness (<s>aprāptakāla</s>), (11) deficiency (<s>nyūna</s>), (12) excess (<s>adhika</s>), (13) repetition (<s>punarukta</s>), (14) failure to respond (<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s>), (15) ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>), (16) lack of wit (<s>apratibhā</s>), (17) evasion (<s>vikṣepa</s>) — that is, avoiding refutation through pretexts, (18) admission of the opponent's charge (<s>matānujñā</s>) — that is, conceding the opponent's refutation, (19) overlooking what should be challenged (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>) — that is, overlooking the incurrence of a point of defeat by one who has incurred it, (20) challenging what need not be challenged (<s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s>) — that is, leveling a charge of defeat where there is no ground for it, (21) deviation from doctrine (<s>apasiddhānta</s>), (22) pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>). These are the twenty-two points of defeat. If anyone incurs a point of defeat, debate should no longer be conducted with that person.

body.text:
1. pratijñāhāniḥ / svapratijñāyāṃ pratipakṣābhyanujñeti pratijñāhāniḥ /
nityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt / amūrtatvāt / ākāśavat / iti sthāpite 'paraḥ prāha / śabda ākāśasādharmyannitya iti cettato yadi vaidharmyaṃ syāt, tadānityaḥ / vaidharmyañca śabdasya sahetukatvamākāśasya tvahetukatvamiti / śabda aindriyaka ākāśastvanaindriyakaḥ / tasmācchabdo 'nitya iti pratyavasthita idamāha / sādharmyaṃ vaidharmyaṃ vā na mayā samālocyate / nityasādharmyaṃ tu mayoktam / yadi nityasadharmā tadā nitya iti /
body.translated_text:
1. Abandonment of the thesis (<s>pratijñāhāni</s>): Conceding the counter-thesis against one's own thesis is abandonment of the thesis.
Sound is permanent. Why? Because of incorporeality (<s>amūrtatva</s>), like space. When this is established, the other says: 'If sound is permanent due to similarity with space, then if there were dissimilarity, it would be impermanent. And the dissimilarity of sound is that it has a cause (<s>sahetuka</s>), while space has no cause (<s>ahetuka</s>). Sound is perceptible to the senses (<s>aindriyaka</s>), while space is not perceptible to the senses. Therefore sound is impermanent.' When thus countered, [the proponent] says: 'I do not consider either similarity or dissimilarity. But I have stated similarity with what is permanent. If [sound] has similarity with the permanent, then it is permanent.'

body.text:
atrāparaḥ / nityasādharmyamanaikāntikam / amūrtānyanityānyapi bastūni vidyante / yathā sukhaduḥkhādīni / tasmādasiddho hetuḥ / vaidharmyaṃ tu sarvamanityaṃ nityavyatiriktamiti niścitaṃ vyanakti / tasmādanityatāsādhane samarthamityukte brūyāt / anityaṃ sahetukam / nityaṃ tvahetukamiti mayāpi pratipāditam / iti pratijñāhāninigrahasthānāpattiḥ /
2. pratijñāntaram / pratijñātārthapratiṣedhe pareṇa kṛte dharmāntaravikalpādarthanirdeśaḥ pratijñāntaramucyate /
body.translated_text:
To this the other [replies]: Similarity with the permanent is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). There are also incorporeal things that are impermanent — such as pleasure, pain, and the like. Therefore the reason is unestablished. But dissimilarity — that all that is impermanent is excluded from the permanent — clearly determines [the matter]. Therefore, when it is said that [dissimilarity] is capable of establishing impermanence, [the proponent] should say: 'What is impermanent has a cause; what is permanent has no cause — this has been demonstrated by me too.' This is the incurrence of the point of defeat called abandonment of the thesis.
2. Shifting the thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>): When the opponent has refuted the originally asserted meaning, [and the proponent] indicates a different meaning through differentiation of properties — this is called shifting the thesis.

body.text: nityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt / asparśatvāt / ākāśavaditi sthāpite aparaḥ prāha / asparśatvahetunā nityaḥ śabda iti bhavatā sthāpitam / asparśatvahetuścānaikāntikaḥ / cittecchakrodhādyasparśamapyanityam / śabdo 'pyasparśastasmādanaikāntikatā / ākāśādivannityaścittādivadanityo vetyasparśatvamanaikāntikameva / tasmādbhavaddheturasiddhaḥ / yadi heturasiddhastadā pratijñāpyasiddheti prasiddhamiti pratyavasthita idamāha / śabdo nityatā ceti na mama pratijñā / api tu nityatā śabdena saṃbaddhā, śabdaśca nityatathā sambaddha ityasmatpratijñā / yo mayā nirdiṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ sa rūpādiniṣedhārthaḥ /
body.translated_text: Sound is permanent. Why? Because of being intangible (<s>asparśatva</s>), like space. When this is established, the other says: 'You have established that sound is permanent by the reason of intangibility. But the reason of intangibility is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). Mind, desire, anger, and the like are intangible yet impermanent. Sound too is intangible — therefore [intangibility is] inconclusive. Like space etc. it may be permanent, or like mind etc. it may be impermanent — thus intangibility is indeed inconclusive. Therefore your reason is unestablished. If the reason is unestablished, then it is well known that the thesis too is unestablished.' When thus countered, [the proponent] says: 'My thesis is not that sound and permanence [are identical]. Rather, my thesis is that permanence is connected with sound, and sound is connected with permanence. The sound I have indicated is for the purpose of excluding form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like.

body.text: yā ca mayā nirdiṣṭā nityatā, sā nityatāniṣedhārthā / nityatā śabdānna vyatiricyate rūpādibhyastu vyatiricyate / śabdo nityatāyā na vyatiricyate śrotragrāhyādikāttu vyatiricyate / yadyasmānna vyatiricyate, tattena sambaddham, eṣāsmatpratijñā / mayā na śabdo na ca nityatā sthāpyate / bhavān punaḥ śabdañca nityatāñca khaṇḍayati (

children.translated_text: [<s>Tarkaśāstra</s> 35]

children.text: ) na tu mama pratijñāṃ khaṇḍayati / iyamucyate pratijñāntarānagrahasthānāpattiḥ /
children.translated_text: without refuting my thesis.' This is called the incurrence of the point of defeat of shifting the thesis.

body.translated_text: And the permanence I have indicated is for the purpose of excluding impermanence. Permanence is not different from sound, but it is different from form and the like. Sound is not different from permanence, but it is different from what is graspable by the ear and so on. What is not different from [something] is connected with it — this is my thesis. I am establishing neither sound nor permanence [as separate entities]. But you refute both sound and permanence

body.text: 3. pratijñāvirodhaḥ / hetupratijñayorvirodhaḥ pratijñāvirodha ityucyate /
body.translated_text: 3. Contradiction of the thesis (<s>pratijñāvirodha</s>): A contradiction between the reason and the thesis is called contradiction of the thesis.

body.text: prativādī prāha / nityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt / sarvasyānityatvāt / ākāśavat / iti sthāpite 'paraḥ prāha bhavatoktaṃ sarvamanityaṃ tasmānnityaḥ śabda iti / atha śabdaḥ sarvasminnantarbhavati na vā / sarvasminnantarbhavati cet / sarvasyānityatvācchabdo 'pyanityaḥ / sarvasminnāntarbhavati cettadā sarvamityasiddham / kuta iti cet / śabdasyāsaṅgrahāt / hetuvacane pratijñāhāniḥ / pratijñāvacane ca hetuhāniḥ / tasmādbhavato 'rtho 'siddhaḥ / iyaṃ pratijñāvirodhanigrahasthānāpattirucyate /
body.translated_text: The opponent says: Sound is permanent. Why? Because everything is impermanent. Like space. When this is established, the other says: 'You have said that everything is impermanent, therefore sound is permanent. Now, does sound fall within the scope of "everything" or not? If it falls within the scope of "everything," then since everything is impermanent, sound too is impermanent. If it does not fall within the scope of "everything," then "everything" is unestablished. Why? Because sound is not included. In stating the reason, the thesis is abandoned; in stating the thesis, the reason is abandoned. Therefore your position is unestablished.' This is called the incurrence of the point of defeat of contradiction of the thesis.

body.text: 4. pratijñāsaṃnyāsaḥ / pareṇa svapratijñāpratiṣedhe kṛte saṃnyāso 'samarthaneti pratijñāsaṃnyāsaḥ /
body.translated_text: 4. Renunciation of the thesis (<s>pratijñāsaṃnyāsa</s>): When the opponent has refuted one's own thesis and [the proponent] renounces it, being unable [to defend it] — that is renunciation of the thesis.

body.text: nityaḥ śabdaḥ / kutaḥ / aindriyakatvāt / yathā sāmānyamaindriyakaṃ nityañca / śabdo 'pyaindriyakatvānnityaḥ / iti sthāpite 'paraḥ prāha nityaḥ śabda aindriyakatvāditi bhavatoktam / atha yadaindriyakaṃ tadanityalakṣaṇākrāntaṃ ghaṭādivat / ghaṭo hyaindriyakatvādanityaḥ / tasmācchabdopyanitya iti / yadbhavatoktaṃ sāmānyavannityamiti tadayuktam / tathā hi gavādisāmānyaṃ gavāderabhinnaṃ bhinnaṃ vā / abhinnañced, gaureva san sāmānyaṃ tvasat / bhinnañced, gorvyatiriktaṃ sāmānyaṃ prakāśeta na tu gorvyatiriktaṃ sāmānyaṃ prakāśate tasmāddṛṣṭānto na nityatāsādhakaḥ / pratijñā cāsiddhā / (

children.translated_text: [<s>Tarkaśāstra</s> 36]

children.text: ) iti dūṣaṇe kṛte prativādī prāha kenaitatsthāpitam / iyaṃ pratijñāsannyāsanigrahasthānāpattirityucyate /
children.translated_text: When this refutation is made, the opponent says: 'By whom has this been established?' This is called the incurrence of the point of defeat of renunciation of the thesis.

body.translated_text: Sound is permanent. Why? Because of being perceptible to the senses (<s>aindriyakatva</s>). Just as a universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is perceptible to the senses and permanent, sound too, being perceptible to the senses, is permanent. When this is established, the other says: 'You have said that sound is permanent because of being perceptible to the senses. But what is perceptible to the senses is encompassed by the mark of impermanence, like a pot and so on. A pot is impermanent because of being perceptible to the senses. Therefore sound too is impermanent. And your statement that [sound is] permanent like a universal is not proper. For the universal of cow and the like — is it identical with or different from [individual] cows etc.? If identical, then being nothing other than a cow, the universal would be non-existent. If different, a universal distinct from the cow should be manifest — but no universal distinct from the cow is manifest. Therefore the example does not establish permanence, and the thesis is unestablished.'

body.text: 5. hetvantaram / aviśeṣahetau sthāpite paścāddhetvantaroktiriti hetvantaram /
body.translated_text: 5. Shifting the reason (<s>hetvantara</s>): When a non-specific reason is established and afterward a different reason is stated — that is shifting the reason.

body.text: nityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt / dviranabhivyaktatvāt / yannityaṃ tatsarvaṃ sakṛdabhivyaktamākāśavat / śabdasyāpi tathātvam / iti sthāpite 'paraḥ prāha / nityaḥ śabdo dviranabhivyaktatvāt / ākāśavaditi na tveṣa heturyuktaḥ / kuta iti ceddviranabhivyaktasya nityatānaikāntikatvāt / yathā vāyoḥ sparśasya ca sakṛdevābhivaktavāpi vāyuranityaḥ / śabdo 'pi tatheti pratyavasthita idamāha / śabdo vāyuvilakṣaṇaḥ / vāyurhi tvagindriyagrāhyaḥ / śabdastu śravaṇagrāhyaḥ / tasmācchabdo vāyuvilakṣaṇa iti /
body.translated_text: Sound is permanent. Why? Because of not being manifested a second time (<s>dvir-anabhivyaktatva</s>). Whatever is permanent is manifested only once, like space. Sound too is likewise. When this is established, the other says: '[You say] sound is permanent because of not being manifested a second time, like space — but this reason is not proper. Why? Because [the property of] not being manifested a second time is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) with respect to permanence. For wind and touch, though manifested only once, are impermanent. Sound is likewise.' When thus countered, [the proponent] says: 'Sound is unlike wind. For wind is graspable by the tactile sense organ, while sound is graspable by the auditory sense organ. Therefore sound is unlike wind.'

body.text: atrāparaḥ prāha / pūrvamuktaṃ bhavatā śabdo nityo dviranabhivyaktatvādityadhunā tūcyate śabdo vāyuvilakṣaṇaḥ pṛthagindriyagrāhyatvāditi prathamahetutyāgena bhavata hetvantaraṃ pratiṣṭhāpitam / tasmādbhavato heturasiddhaḥ / iyaṃ hetvantaranigrahasthānāpattirucyate /
body.translated_text: To this the other says: 'Previously you said "sound is permanent because of not being manifested a second time," but now you say "sound is unlike wind because of being graspable by a different sense organ." By abandoning the first reason, you have established a different reason. Therefore your reason is unestablished.' This is called the incurrence of the point of defeat of shifting the reason.

body.text: 6. arthāntaram / prakṛtārthāpratisambaddhārthābhidhānamarthāntaram /
body.translated_text: 6. Irrelevant meaning (<s>arthāntara</s>): Stating a meaning that is unconnected with the subject under discussion is irrelevant meaning.

body.text: nityaḥ śabdaḥ / kasmāt / rūpādipañcaskandhā daśahetupratyayāḥ / etaducyate arthāntaram /
body.translated_text: Sound is permanent. Why? The five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) of form etc. [arise from] the ten causes and conditions. This is called irrelevant meaning.

body.text: 7. nirarthakam / yadā vāda iṣṭastadā mantrabhāṣaṇamiti nirarthakiam /
body.translated_text: 7. Meaninglessness (<s>nirarthaka</s>): When a debate is undertaken, [resorting to] the recitation of mantras — that is meaninglessness.

body.text: 8. avijñātārtham / pariṣatprativādibhyāṃ trirabhihitamapyavijñātamityavijñātārtham /
body.translated_text: 8. Unintelligible meaning (<s>avijñātārtha</s>): What is not understood by the assembly and the opponent even after being stated three times — that is unintelligible meaning.

body.text: yadi kaściddharmaṃ vakti pariṣattu prativādī ca jijñāsāvapi trirabhihitaṃ jñātumasamarthau / yathā (kaścidvaded) aṇuramūrtaḥ sukhotpādakaḥ duḥkhotpādako 'prāpto sāpakarṣotkarṣaḥ samito 'sannyāso na vināśaḥ / śabdo nityaḥ kasmāt / anityasya nityatvāt / iyamavijñātārthanigrahasthānāpattirucyate /
body.translated_text: If someone states a doctrine, but the assembly and the opponent, even wishing to understand, are unable to understand it even after it has been stated three times — for example, [if someone were to say:] 'An atom is incorporeal, a producer of pleasure, a producer of pain, not reached, possessed of attraction and repulsion, quiescent, not renounced, not destroyed. Sound is permanent. Why? Because of the permanence of the impermanent.' This is called the incurrence of the point of defeat of unintelligible meaning.

body.text: 9. apārthakam / paurvāparyyāsambandho 'pārthakam / yathā kaścidvadet / daśavidhaṃ phalaṃ trividhaḥ kaṃbala ekavidhaṃ pānabhojanametadapārthakamucyate /
body.translated_text: 9. Incoherence (<s>apārthaka</s>): Lack of connection between what precedes and what follows is incoherence. For example, if someone were to say: 'Fruit is of ten kinds, a blanket is of three kinds, food and drink is of one kind' — this is called incoherence.

body.text: 10. aprāptakālam / pratijñāyāṃ duṣṭāyāṃ paścāddhetusthāpanamaprāptakālam /
body.translated_text: 10. Untimeliness (<s>aprāptakāla</s>): Establishing a reason after the thesis has been shown to be defective is untimeliness.

body.text: nityaḥ śabdaḥ / yathā pārimāṇḍalyāśrayasya paramāṇornityatvātpārimāṇḍalyaṃ nityaṃ śabdasyāpi tathātvasambhava iti kṛte 'paraḥ prāha / bhavatā nityatāsthāpane heturnoktaḥ, pañcāvayavanyūnavacanasthāpanādbhavadartho 'siddha iti dūṣita idaṃ prāha / asti me heturnāmnā tu noktaḥ / ko 'yaṃ heturiti cet / nityākāśāśrayatvamiti /
body.translated_text: Sound is permanent. Just as the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>) that is the substrate of sphericity (<s>pārimāṇḍalya</s>) is permanent, sphericity is permanent; the possibility of sound being likewise — when this is put forth, the other says: 'You have not stated a reason for establishing permanence; because of your establishing [the thesis] with a statement lacking the five members (<s>pañcāvayava</s>), your position is unestablished.' When thus refuted, [the proponent] says: 'I do have a reason, but I have not stated it by name. What is this reason? It is the property of being the substrate of permanent space (<s>nityākāśāśrayatva</s>).'

body.text: atrāparaḥ / yathā gṛhe dagdhe tatparitrāṇāyodakānveṣaṇaṃ tathānavasare 'rtharakṣaṇāya hetusthāpanam / etadaprāptakālamucyate /
body.translated_text: Here is another [illustration]: Just as when a house is on fire, one searches for water to protect it, so too is the establishment of a reason for preserving one's thesis when it is no longer timely. This is called untimely [argument].

body.text: 11. nyūnam / pañcāvayavā anyatamena hīnā iti nyūnam / pratijñā heturudāharaṇamupanayanaṃ nigamanamiti pañcāvayavāḥ /
body.translated_text: 11. <s>Nyūna</s> (deficiency). Being deficient in any one of the five members—this is called deficiency. The five members are: <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis), <s>hetu</s> (reason), <s>udāharaṇa</s> (example), <s>upanayana</s> (application), and <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion).

body.text: yathā (kaścidvadatya) nityaḥ śabda ityayaṃ prathamo 'vayavaḥ / kṛtakatvāditi dvitīyo 'vayavaḥ / yadvastu kṛtakaṃ tadanityaṃ yathā ghaṭaḥ kṛtako 'nityaśceti tṛtīyo 'vayavaḥ / śabdo 'pi tatheti caturtho 'vayavaḥ / tasmācchabdo 'nitya iti pañcamo 'vayavaḥ / pañcāvayavānāmanyatamena nyūnatā nyūnanigrahasthānāpattirityucyate /
body.translated_text: For example, (someone says) 'Sound is permanent'—this is the first member. 'Because of being produced'—this is the second member. 'Whatever thing is produced, that is impermanent, like a pot—a pot is produced and impermanent'—this is the third member. 'Sound is also like that'—this is the fourth member. 'Therefore sound is impermanent'—this is the fifth member. Deficiency in any one of these five members incurs the defeat-situation of deficiency.

body.text: 12. adhikam / bahuhetūdāharaṇoktiradhikam / yathā (kaścidvade) cchabdo 'nityaḥ / kasmāt? / prayatnānantarīyakatvādamūrtatvādaindriyakatvādutpādavināśābhyāṃ vācyatvāccaitaddhetubāhulyamityucyate / api ca śabdo 'nityaḥ kṛtakatvād ghaṭavatpaṭavatgṛhavatkarmmavat / etaddṛṣṭāntabāhulyamityucyate /
body.translated_text: 12. <s>Adhika</s> (excess). The statement of multiple reasons and examples is called excess. For example, (someone says) 'Sound is impermanent. Why? Because of being subsequent to effort, because of being formless, because of being perceptible by the senses, and because it can be described by origination and destruction'—this is called excess of reasons. Furthermore, 'Sound is impermanent because of being produced—like a pot, like a cloth, like a house, like an action'—this is called excess of examples.

body.text: vādī prāha / bhavatā hetūdāharaṇabahulyamuktam / yadyeko hetuḥ sādhanāsamarthastadā kathamekahetuprayogaḥ / atha sādhanasamarthastadā kiṃ hetubāhulyena udāharaṇabahulye 'pi tathātvasambhavaḥ / tadbāhulyokteraprayojanatvāt /
body.translated_text: The proponent says: You have spoken of excess of reasons and examples. If one reason is incapable of proving, then how can the use of a single reason [suffice]? But if it is capable of proving, then what is the need for multiple reasons? The same possibility applies to excess of examples. Because stating them in excess is purposeless.

body.text: 13. punaruktam / punaruktaṃ trividhaṃ, śabdapunaruktaṃ, artha punaruktaṃ, arthāpattipunaruktañca / śabdapunaruktaṃ yathā (kaścidvade) cchakraḥ śakraḥ / arthapunaruktaṃ yathā (kaścidvadet) cakṣurakṣi / arthāpattipunaruktaṃ yathā (kaścidvadet) satyaṃ saṃsāro duḥkhaṃ satyaṃ nirvāṇaṃ sukham / prathamameva vacanaṃ vaktavyaṃ dvitīyaṃ tvaprayojanam / kasmāt / pūrvavacanasya spaṣṭārthatvāt / pūrvavacanasyārtha spaṣṭaśced, dvitīyavacanena kiṃ spaṣṭaṃ bhavet / yadi na kiñcit prakaṭayitavyaṃ tadā tadaprayojanam / etatpunaruktamityucyate /
body.translated_text: 13. <s>Punarukta</s> (repetition). Repetition is threefold: verbal repetition, repetition of meaning, and repetition by implication. Verbal repetition: for example, (someone says) '<s>Śakra</s>, <s>Śakra</s>.' Repetition of meaning: for example, (someone says) '<s>cakṣu</s>, <s>akṣi</s>' (both meaning 'eye'). Repetition by implication: for example, (someone says) 'Truly, <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) is suffering; truly, <s>nirvāṇa</s> (liberation) is happiness.' Only the first statement needs to be made; the second is purposeless. Why? Because the meaning of the first statement is clear. If the meaning of the first statement is clear, what would be made clear by the second statement? If nothing is to be made evident, then it is purposeless. This is called repetition.

body.text: 14. ananubhāṣaṇam / pariṣadā vijñātāyāḥ pratijñāyāstrirabhihitāyā (

children.translated_text: is not able to be repeated by someone, that is failure to repeat.

body.translated_text: 14. <s>Ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (failure to repeat). When a thesis that has been understood by the assembly and stated three times

body.text: 15. ajñānam / pariṣadā vijñātāyā api pratijñāyāḥ kenacidavijñānamajñānamucyate /
body.translated_text: 15. <s>Ajñāna</s> (ignorance). When someone does not understand a thesis that has been understood by the assembly, this is called ignorance.

body.text: 16. apratibhā / yadi parasya pratijñāṃ nyāyavadīkṣate dūṣaṇe cāsamarthastadāpratibhā /
body.translated_text: 16. <s>Apratibhā</s> (lack of readiness). If one sees the opponent's thesis as reasonable but is incapable of refuting it, that is lack of readiness.

body.text: apare tu vadanti / ajñāne 'pratibhāyāñcobhayatrānigrahasthānāpattiḥ / kasmāt? / yadi kaścidarthaṃ na vijānāti dūṣaṇe cāsamarthastena saha vādo na kartavya iti /
body.translated_text: Others, however, say: in both ignorance and lack of readiness, there is no defeat-situation. Why? Because if someone does not understand the meaning and is incapable of refutation, one should not engage in debate with such a person.

body.text: ete tvatimande nigrahasthāne / anyeṣu nigrahasthāneṣu, sadoṣasya vacanasya vividhenopāyenoddharaṇaṃ śakyam / atra tūbhayatra na kaścidupāya uddharaṇasamarthaḥ / eṣa manuṣyaḥ pūrvaṃ pāṇḍityagauravaṃ sthāpayati, paścāttu pāṇḍityaṃ prakaṭayitumaśaktaḥ /
body.translated_text: These two are the most extreme defeat-situations. In other defeat-situations, it is possible to rescue a faulty statement by various means. But in these two cases, there is no means capable of rescue. Such a person first establishes the prestige of his learning, but afterward is unable to display that learning.

body.text: 17. vikṣepaḥ / svapratijñāyā doṣaṃ jñātvā vyājaiḥ parihāraḥ kāryāntarakathanam / yathāhaṃ svayaṃ rogī, ahaṃ paraṃ roginaṃ draṣṭumicchāmi / tadā tu yadi nāpakrāmati paradūṣaṇanirākaraṇaṃ na kalpayati / kasmāt / bandhusnehāpagamabhayāt / iti vikṣepanigrahasthānāpattirucyate /
body.translated_text: 17. <s>Vikṣepa</s> (evasion). Knowing the fault of one's own thesis, making excuses and speaking of other matters as an escape. For example, 'I myself am sick; I wish to visit another sick person.' If at that time one does not depart and does not devise a way to counter the opponent's refutation—why? Because of fear of losing the affection of relatives—this incurs the defeat-situation of evasion.

body.text: 18. matānujñā / paradūṣaṇe svapakṣadoṣābhyupagama iti matānujñā / yadi kaścit pareṇa dūṣaṇe kṛte, svapakṣadoṣamanujānāti, yathā mama doṣa evaṃ bhavato 'pītyabhyupagacchan / iyaṃ matānujñocyate /
body.translated_text: 18. <s>Matānujñā</s> (concession to the opponent). Acknowledging the fault of one's own position when the opponent has made a refutation—this is called concession. If someone, when a refutation has been made by the opponent, concedes the fault of their own position, saying 'Just as the fault is mine, so it is yours too'—this is called concession.

body.text: 19. paryanuyojyopekṣaṇam / yadi kaścinnigrahasthānaṃ prāpnuyāt, tasya nigrahāpattyanudbhāvanaṃ taddūṣaṇecchayā tu (

children.text: ) dūṣaṇasthāpanam / tadarthe ca hīne kiṃ prayojanaṃ dūṣaṇena / asiddhametaddūṣaṇam / etaducyate paryanuyojyopekṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: a [different] refutation is established—and if that purpose is deficient, what use is the refutation? This refutation is unestablished. This is called ignoring what deserves censure.

body.translated_text: 19. <s>Paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s> (ignoring what deserves censure). If someone incurs a defeat-situation, and the raising of that defeat is neglected, but instead, out of desire to refute,

body.text: 20. niranuyojyānuyogaḥ / kasyacidanigrāhyatve 'pi nigrahasthānābhiyogo niranuyojyānuyogaḥ / anyacca / prativādini svapratijñāhānyāpanne svapakṣabhinnārthopādānenāsthāne paranigrahasthānadyotanam / ayamapi niranuyojyānuyogaḥ /
body.translated_text: 20. <s>Niranuyojyānuyoga</s> (censuring what does not deserve censure). Charging someone with a defeat-situation even when they are not subject to defeat—this is censuring what does not deserve censure. And further: when the opponent has incurred the abandonment of their own thesis, illuminating a defeat-situation in the wrong place by adopting a meaning different from one's own position—this too is censuring what does not deserve censure.

body.text: 21. apasiddhāntaḥ / pūrvaṃ caturvidhe siddhānte svayamaṅgīkṛte 'pi paścāccedyathāsiddhāntaṃ na brūyādayamapasiddhāntaḥ /
body.translated_text: 21. <s>Apasiddhānta</s> (contradiction of one's own doctrine). If one has previously accepted one of the four types of established doctrine, but afterward does not speak in accordance with that doctrine—this is contradiction of one's own doctrine.

body.text: 22. hetvābhāsāḥ / yathā pūrvamuktāstrividhāḥ / asiddho 'neikāntiko viruddhaśceti hetvābhāsāḥ /
body.translated_text: 22. <s>Hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons). As stated before, they are threefold: <s>asiddha</s> (unestablished), <s>anaikāntika</s> (inconclusive), and <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory)—these are the fallacious reasons.

body.text: asiddhaḥ / yathā kaścit sthāpayedaśva āgacchati / kasmāt / śṛṅgadarśanāt / aśvo 'śṛṅga iti śṛṅgaheturasiddho 'śvāgamanasthāpanāsamarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Asiddha</s> (unestablished): For example, someone establishes 'A horse is coming. Why? Because of seeing horns.' Since a horse is hornless, the reason of horns is unestablished and incapable of establishing the arrival of a horse.

body.text: anaikāntikaḥ / yathā kaścit sthāpayetgaurāgacchati / kasmāt / śṛṅgadarśanāt / yaḥ saśṛṅga sa gaurityanaikāntikaḥ chāgarurvādīnāṃ saśṛṅgatvāt / śṛṅgaheturanaikāntikaḥ / tasmādgavāgamanasthāpanāsamarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Anaikāntika</s> (inconclusive): For example, someone establishes 'A cow is coming. Why? Because of seeing horns.' That whatever has horns is a cow—this is inconclusive, because goats, deer, and others also have horns. The reason of horns is inconclusive. Therefore it is incapable of establishing the arrival of a cow.

body.text: viruddhaḥ / yathā kaścit sthāpayetprabhāte rātriḥ / kasmāt / aruṇodayāt / aruṇodayo rātryā viruddhaḥ / aruṇodayahetū rātristhāpanāsamarthaḥ / yadi kenacideṣa hetuḥ prayujyate tadā hetvābhāsanigrahasthānāpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Viruddha</s> (contradictory): For example, someone establishes 'It is night at dawn. Why? Because of the rising of the dawn.' The rising of the dawn is contradictory to night. The reason of the rising of the dawn is incapable of establishing night. If someone uses such a reason, then the defeat-situation of a fallacious reason is incurred.

body.text:
iti tṛtīyaṃ prakaraṇam /
samāptaścāyaṃ grantha /
body.translated_text:
Thus ends the third chapter.
And this treatise is complete.
